Posture is what delivers the technology. It also makes the build spec non-negotiable, and yours is confirmed: 34", set flat. SECOND — more bend lets the arms hang freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall flattens that plane and builds an arc into the stroke whether you want one or not. Your stroke is SBST on film. The deep bend is the posture that matches it.
sections.k: The bend isn't comfort: it presents the lie the putter needs, and steepens the shoulder plane that makes the stroke straight.

sections.t: The setup
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. Ball off the LEFT BREAST. Weight stacked ON the ball — pressure over it, not on the trail foot. TRAIL FOOT a touch BACK — it creeps forward on its own and opens you. Rock the shoulders, no hands. Loose grip.

THE HANDS CUE REVERTS. HANDS EVEN WITH THE BALL; the grip's built-in 2° supplies the lean. That was the cue for the whole DF3i era and it is correct again now the Press Pistol is back under your hands.

It's worth understanding why it went away, because the reasoning was sound and it simply doesn't apply to this grip. On the LINK's Pistol 0 there is no built-in press, and overhead stills measured Jul 30 showed the shaft sitting essentially vertical with the hands about 1.35" BEHIND the centre of the ball. That's pure geometry: with the face resting against the ball, the ball's centre is half a ball ahead of the face, and on a heel-shafted putter the shaft axis sits roughly another half inch behind that. A vertical shaft can't put the hands anywhere else. With a Pistol 0 you cannot have hands-over-ball AND a vertical shaft.

The Press Pistol changes the arithmetic by leaning the shaft for you — which is the entire point of a pressed grip. So hands even is reachable again, and it is what this putter was set up around. Don't carry 'hands over the clubhead' across: on a 2° grip that stacks lean on top of lean.
sections.k: Hands EVEN with the ball — the Press Pistol's built-in 2° supplies the lean, so you don't.

sections.t: THE PRESS — settled from first principles
sections.b:
Start from what you are actually holding. The Press Pistol 2° is a PRESSED grip — the 2° is built-in forward lean, delivered the same way on every putt whether you're calm or not. That is a genuinely good deal on a lie-angle-balanced putter: the premise is a head that squares itself when the shaft is presented at its designed lie and the hands stop interfering, and a grip that supplies the lean is a lean your hands don't have to invent.

So the recommendation is: DO NOT add lean with your hands. Not as a matter of taste — as arithmetic. Starting from 2° of built-in lean, a firm press pushes effective loft off the bottom of the scale, and a putter delivering negative loft drives the ball down into the green instead of rolling it. That produces a hop, then a skid, then roll, and the skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your PACE stops being repeatable. Pace is the open fault.

This is the rule that went quiet during the LINK fortnight, because a Pistol 0 has no lean to double-count and a small press could only move you toward normal loft. That relaxation is over. Keep a trigger if it helps you start the motion — a soft press moved with the body is fine, and its job is RHYTHM only. But on this grip, small isn't a preference. It's the safeguard.
sections.k: The grip already leaned it. Don't add more with your hands — that's how loft goes below zero.

sections.t: What this putter needs from the setup
sections.b:
A lie-angle-balanced putter makes one demand of you and it is not a stroke demand: present the shaft at the lie it was built for. Get that wrong — stand tall, reach for it — and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its designed lie, and the self-squaring property you bought degrades. That is why the deep bend matters mechanically here and not just for comfort.

Everything else in this routine came from film of YOUR stroke — path, shoulder plane, stance line, trigger — so none of it is putter-specific and none of it changes. Two things ARE this head's business. The lie presentation above. And your AIM PICTURE: a wide mallet topline frames the target differently from the narrow blade you've spent two weeks looking at, and start line is the open fault. Re-run the alignment-stick check in your first DF3i session and don't assume aim carried over — that's true in both directions, and you've now changed sight lines twice in a fortnight.
sections.k: Present the shaft at its built lie and re-check your aim picture. Leave the stroke alone.

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — the alignment leak
sections.b: Self-reported Jul 29 and worth taking seriously: your right foot creeps UP — forward, toward the target line — and it drags the stance line open with it. Open the feet and the shoulders follow, so you end up aimed LEFT of where you think you are. The fix is exactly what you said: set that trail foot a touch further back than feels natural. Expect it to feel CLOSED, like you're aimed right. That feeling is the correction, not an error — you're recalibrating off an open baseline, so square will read as closed until it beds in. Trust the line you set, not the feel, for the first few sessions.
sections.k: Your trail foot creeps forward, opens the stance and aims you left. Set it back — square will feel closed.

sections.t: Why it wrecks the takeaway specifically
sections.b: Because in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. There's no arc to absorb a misaligned setup — 'straight back' is straight back along whatever line your shoulders are on, so an open stance doesn't just aim you left, it points the whole stroke left. Then one of two things happens, and both are bad: you feel it immediately and manipulate the takeaway to save it, which puts the HANDS back in charge of a stroke built to have no hands in it — or you don't, and the ball starts left. That's why a stance error shows up as a takeaway problem. The takeaway is fine; it's obeying a line that's wrong.
sections.k: In a straight stroke the shoulder line IS the track, so an open stance points the whole stroke left.

sections.t: This is the miss the putter can't fix
sections.b:
Your signature miss is LEFT on short putts — the through-line of the entire putter saga, and it showed up AGAIN on the course Jul 29 with a zero-torque putter in your hands. That is the most useful data point you've generated in weeks, because it rules the head out, and the fact that it has now outlived three putters says the same thing louder. A perfectly square face aimed at a target that's left of the hole produces precisely that miss, and no putter ever built will save you from it. Zero-torque guarantees the FACE stays square; it cannot guarantee the face is square TO THE RIGHT THING.

Note the split that makes the case: your last two 10-ball blocks started 10/10 on line on the mat, and then you pulled it on grass. Stance creep is a course-and-pressure fault — mat reps are exactly where it wouldn't show. And one thing to redo now the mallet is back: you've changed sight lines again. Re-run the alignment-stick check in your first DF3i session rather than assuming the aim you built on the blade transfers.
sections.k: A square face aimed at the wrong target still misses left, and no putter can fix that.

sections.t: The check that costs nothing
sections.b: Lay a club or an alignment stick down the target line just outside the ball on the practice green and set up to it — your toes should run PARALLEL to it, not converging toward it. Ten seconds, and it recalibrates the feel. The structural safeguard is already in your routine: aim the FACE to the spot FIRST, then build the stance around it. Keep that order religiously. If you build the stance first, the face gets aimed to a crooked body; if you aim the face first and the stance then creeps, the mismatch shows up as discomfort — and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.
sections.k: Alignment stick on the practice green: toes parallel, not converging. Ten seconds, recalibrates the feel.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — settled: soft press, moved with the body
sections.b:
Keep the soft press — a genuinely small one, made as the body starts to move. Its JOB is rhythm: it breaks inertia so the stroke starts as a motion rather than a decision.

What it is NOT, on this grip, is the source of your forward lean. The Press Pistol's 2° is already there. So any press you add is a SURPLUS on top of lean that's already built in — which is exactly why 'keep it tiny' was such a hard rule through the DF3i era, and why the held press on Jul 29 was a real problem rather than a stylistic one.

For two weeks that warning was suspended, correctly: on the LINK's Pistol 0 there was no built-in lean, the press was the only lean in the stroke, and a small one could not stack loft off the bottom of the scale. That putter is in storage. The warning is back on.
sections.k: Keep the soft press for rhythm — but on this grip it's a surplus on top of 2°, so it stays small.

sections.t: The one rule — softness IS the safeguard
sections.b:
REINSTATED Aug 2. The rule exists because the press adds lean on top of a grip that already has 2° built in — so a firm press pushes the effective loft below zero and the ball gets driven into the turf instead of rolled. That arithmetic went away with the Pistol 0 and came straight back with the Press Pistol.

So the rule is SMALL and CONSISTENT, both: same press, same size, every putt. A press that varies is a loft that varies, which is a PACE that varies — and pace is the fault with the least evidence against it. Two drift signals to watch: if it starts to feel FIRM, or like a POSITION you sit in rather than a motion you pass through, it has crept back toward a hold.
sections.k: Small AND consistent: the grip's 2° means a press that grows pushes loft below zero.

sections.t: If it creeps back into a hold
sections.b: The alternatives stay on the shelf rather than getting deleted, because you may want one later: THE FLOAT — lift the head a hair off the turf before takeaway; no hand action at all and it removes ground friction. THE WHOLE-PUTTER WAGGLE — small forward-and-back from the shoulders, wrists silent. THE LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE — a soft downward press of the shoulder that already runs the stroke. THE TRAIL-KNEE KICK — furthest from the hands, and the same trigger your full-swing routine uses. Any of them will break inertia without the hands touching shaft lean. You don't need one right now.
sections.k: Alternatives on the shelf if the press ever creeps back into a hold — float, waggle, shoulder settle, knee kick.

sections.t: How to tell it's releasing
sections.b: One face-on clip settles it: compare shaft lean at ADDRESS with shaft lean at IMPACT. Close to equal means the soft press is passing through the way it should. Meaningfully more at impact means it's being carried in, whatever it felt like — and feel is exactly what got this wrong the first time. The free check needs no camera: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click, a ball driven down into the green adds a faint scuff a beat later. Listen for the scuff.
sections.k: One face-on clip settles it: shaft lean at address versus at impact. No camera? Listen for the scuff.

sections.t: Stop shopping
sections.b:
Straight talk, because you called it yourself. That was three putters in a month, and the DF3i originally got 12 days and not one calibrated lag session before you convicted it. Twelve days isn't enough to convict a putter — it's enough to convict a power curve you never built.

It's now back in the bag on the strength of one scramble, which is thin in the other direction, but it lands on the right head: the one you've putted your best with, still zero-torque, still no proven fault against it. The LINK didn't fail either — it lost on redundancy, and owning two zero-torque L.A.B. putters was the real mistake.

So the head is settled and the rule from here is simple: the next thing that changes is a NUMBER on the card, not a putter in the bag. Keep the stroke frozen — the deep bend and the soft press were both decided from clear feel and both are mechanically sound. One variable at a time, and this time the variable is the lag ladder.
sections.k: Three putters in a month, now settled. The next thing that changes is a number, not a head.

sections.t: Why beside the ball and not behind it
sections.b: Rehearsing in your true putting posture — same deep bend, same arm hang, same shoulder plane — means the stroke that FEELS like 30 feet is the stroke you actually make. Magnitude transfers one-to-one. Rehearsing from behind the ball reads the break better, but you're standing upright there, so the size you feel is only an approximation. Your open fault is pace magnitude, not reading: path ✓, face ✓, start lines 10/10 twice over. Optimise the thing that's broken.
sections.k: Rehearse in your real posture beside the ball, because magnitude transfers one-to-one that way.

sections.t: Keep the order of the two rehearsals
sections.b: Ball-look first (path and contact), hole-look second (pace). The last thing you feel is the thing you carry in — so the pace stroke must be the last one. If the hole stroke ever drifts to first, the pace feel gets overwritten by the contact feel and you're back to guessing distance. Finish rehearsal 2 WITH the soft press, at its real size: it's the one part of the stroke that never used to get a practice rep, which is how it drifted last time without you noticing.
sections.k: Ball-look first, hole-look second — the last thing you feel is what you carry in.

sections.t: Two rules underneath it
sections.b: SAME BEAT COUNT, EVERY PUTT — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts where you take an extra look are the ones that come up short. And a VERBAL BACKSTOP is worth testing: say the pace intention right before the press ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays, a word doesn't.
sections.k: Same beat count every putt, and try saying the pace intention out loud before the press.

sections.t: Still to test — lags
sections.b:
This is no longer a someday item — it's the top of the card, and it is the single thing that would have prevented the entire detour. The Jul 29 round was lags coming up SHORT and short putts running HOT, which is not two faults but one: a power curve you hadn't learned, so you under-hit the long ones and over-hit the short ones. That is what got the DF3i benched, and it was never once tested against the head.

The DF3i is back and its curve is still unbuilt, so the reps have to be deliberate. The block test, twice a week: 10 balls from 30 feet, and measure the SPREAD of stopping points plus how many finish short. Target no more than 1 in 10 short.

Then the experiment worth running while you're there — past ~25 feet, keep your eyes ON THE HOLE through the actual stroke, not just the rehearsal. Feels absurd, works well; the ball isn't moving, you don't need to watch it. 10 eyes-on-ball vs 10 eyes-on-hole, same session, compare the spreads.
sections.k: Past 25 feet, test keeping your eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke. Block test, not mid-round.

steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. Finish it with the soft press.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot first, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → soft press with the body → putt
rules: GET LOW — the deep bend is what presents the lie this putter needs
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
Hands EVEN with the ball — the Press Pistol's 2° supplies the lean
Keep the press TINY — the grip already leaned it for you
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it

briefing.focus: You feel better with the weight BACK while the ball sits off the front foot — and you've heard the weight is supposed to be forward. Here's what that combination actually costs you, why it lands squarely on the one putting fault still open on your card, and how to settle it with evidence instead of dogma. UPDATED Aug 2 for the DF3i's return: the mallet's high MOI forgives a wandering low point more than the blade did, so the stakes come back down — but the mechanism below is unchanged, and pace is still the open fault.

sections.t: What 'weight forward' is actually for
sections.b: It isn't a rule for its own sake. Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the putter meets the ball. That's the whole mechanism — everything below follows from it, on any head.
sections.k: Lead-side pressure does one job: it pins where the stroke bottoms out.

sections.t: The cost — loft, hop, skid, short
sections.b: Ball off the FRONT foot is correct. But weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so by the time the putter arrives the head is climbing hard and the shaft is leaning AWAY from the target. That adds loft you never asked for. The ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then starts rolling. Every bit of that hop is energy that was supposed to become roll — so the putt arrives soft. Worse, the skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your PACE stops being repeatable from green to green.
sections.k: Hanging back adds loft, and added loft makes the ball hop, skid and arrive short.

sections.t: Why this is your fault, specifically
sections.b: Read the card. Path: settled. Face: settled. Start line: 10/10 clean, twice over. The ONE thing still open is pace — lags coming up short at Hudson Hills, arrivals dying on the mat, and both genuine misses in the Stage-0 4-footer block DIED at the hole. Hop-and-skid off a back-weighted low point is the textbook cause of exactly that signature. Your stroke is no longer the problem. Your strike quality might be.
sections.k: Pace is your one open fault, which is exactly what a wandering low point damages.

sections.t: The second cost — the pull
sections.b: Sitting back drops the trail shoulder and slides your EYELINE behind the ball. Eyes behind the ball make you see the line right of where it truly is, and you square it up with a whisker of pull. Both real misses in the Stage-0 block settled on the PULL side — logged there as a lean, not proof. This belongs on that candidate-cause list.
sections.k: Weight back also leaves the face open through impact — a second route to a missed line.

sections.t: The third cost — the flip can come back
sections.b: Hanging back leaves the hands behind the ball through impact. Hands behind = the wrists want to save it = a flick. That flick was the engine of the old blow-through left miss. Zero-torque has buried that miss on film across two heads now — but hands-behind is the one setup that can wake it up, and the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° makes it worse rather than better: the grip is leaning the shaft forward while your hands hang back behind it, and something has to give.
sections.k: Hands behind the ball invite a wrist flick, the old engine of the blow-through miss.

sections.t: Before changing anything — feel isn't real
sections.b: Your own Golf Mind note states the principle: 'Hands over the ball: it FEELS like a forward press, but it isn't.' The same illusion runs in reverse. Weight that FEELS back is often pressure that's actually close to neutral — and neutral may be perfectly fine. Don't discard a setup you putt well from on the strength of a feel. FILM IT FACE-ON first. That single clip also closes the early-lift fault, the last open item from Session 8.
sections.k: Feel isn't evidence. Film it before you change anything, because comfort lies.

sections.t: What has to be true (the real checklist)
sections.b: Forget 'weight forward' as a slogan. Four things actually matter, and you can keep your comfort as long as they hold. (1) STERNUM at or just ahead of the ball. (2) HANDS level with or a touch ahead of the ball at impact — never behind it. (3) LOW POINT at or just behind the ball, so the head is a HAIR ascending at contact — that slight upstroke is what produces true roll. (4) PRESSURE around 55/45 lead — enough to anchor the low point, not so much that you start steering. If your weight-back feel still delivers 1 through 3, keep it.
sections.k: Four things must be true: sternum over the ball, hands never behind, low point at or just behind it, 55/45 lead.

sections.t: One thing in your favor
sections.b:
The head is back on your side. The DF3i is a wide, deep, heavy mallet: high MOI, self-squaring, happy to be swung rather than steered, and genuinely forgiving of a low point that wanders. For two weeks this section said the opposite, and it was right at the time — a narrow blade carries far less MOI, so a strike off the middle bled more distance and every instruction above carried more weight. That putter is in storage.

So the stakes come down, and none of the instructions change. Low point pinned at or just behind the ball, hands never behind it: on a blade those were the difference between a lag that finishes and one that dies four feet short; on the mallet they're worth a little consistency. Take the forgiveness — it's a real reason this is the right head for you.

But know what you're trading for it. A blade REPORTS a bad strike; a mallet MUFFLES it. The DF3i will let a mediocre low point feel fine, which means feel is a weaker instrument here than it was two weeks ago. That is precisely the argument for the ladder and the tape test below: on this putter, the numbers know things your hands don't.
sections.k: The mallet does cover for you — which is a real gift and a reason to measure rather than trust the feel.

sections.t: Settle it with data
sections.b:
A/B LAG LADDER — 30 feet, two blocks of 10. Block A: your current feel. Block B: the change you're testing, everything else identical. Mark where each ball STOPS and measure the spread. Tighter spread wins — that's the answer, not anyone's opinion. SOUND TEST: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a hopping ball adds a faint scuff a beat later — listen for the scuff. FACE-ON CLIP: check shaft lean at impact and where the head bottoms out relative to the ball, and note that on the Press Pistol 2° you should already see lean at address — the question is whether it holds or grows.

The weight question itself is already settled on the mat (ball off the left breast, weight stacked ON the ball), so this ladder is the measuring protocol for any future change rather than an open question. One amendment as of Aug 2: the head changed back, and the DF3i's power curve was never built in its first 12 days. So the ladder is the FIRST thing that gets run, not a follow-up — you're building this putter's distance baseline from scratch either way, and you may as well build it with the low point in the right place instead of calibrating around a fault.
sections.k: A/B it on the mat and let the stopping points decide, not the feel.

rules: Lead-side pressure has ONE job: pinning the low point
Sternum over the ball, hands NEVER behind it at impact
Low point at or just behind the ball = true roll
The mallet muffles a bad strike — measure it, don't feel it

briefing.focus: Jack's own swing thoughts & setup keys, in his words — the go-to reference before a round or a range session. Grip settled: conventional. Putting routine locked Jul 28; putter settled Aug 1 — DF3i.

sections.t: Driver — the big stick
sections.b: Aim the CENTER of the fairway — the start line tends to pull left, so center-aim leaves room. The straight ball comes from a LONGER, fuller swing — commit to that one. A tighter, shorter swing turns it into a cut, and when that goes wrong the miss is a PUSH-SLICE. So: full swing for straight; if you shorten it, expect the cut and know the push-slice is the bad one.
sections.k: Aim centre — your start line pulls left, and the straight ball needs a LONGER swing, not a tighter one.

sections.t: Mini driver
sections.b: Club setup: the r7 Quad's adjustable WEIGHTS are set in the BACK position. Tee it LOW for the piercing straight ball — NEVER at normal driver-tee height. From that setup you can work it both ways, draw or fade. This is the fairway-finder off the tee; weights back + low tee is what makes it behave.
sections.k: Weights back, teed LOW for the piercing ball. This is the fairway-finder, not a second driver.

sections.t: Irons
sections.b: Ball position right of center, toward the trail (right) thigh. The new KING TECs fly HIGHER and longer than the old set — trust the extra height. When you need to flight it down or take something off, CHOKE DOWN and hit the control shot rather than just swinging soft.
sections.k: Ball back toward the trail thigh; the KING TECs fly higher than the old set, so trust the height.

sections.t: Wedges
sections.b: (Open — fill in as you dial the Vokeys: your go-to feels for full vs. partial, and any open-face/flop keys. Ladder to stay honest: 60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122.)
sections.k: Open — fill in your Vokey feels as you dial them. Ladder: 60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122.

sections.t: Putting — DF3i
sections.b: Ball off the LEFT BREAST — chest reference, not foot: the arc centers on your sternum, so the cue survives a change in stance width. WEIGHT STACKED ON THE BALL — that's what pins the low point. Rock the SHOULDERS, no hands. LOOSE grip. HANDS EVEN with the ball at address: the Press Pistol 2° grip supplies the lean, so you don't add any. (The 'hands over the clubhead, 1.35" behind the ball' cue measured Jul 30 belonged to the LINK's Pistol 0 grip — it's retired with that putter.) The PRESS is a separate trigger that starts the stroke — keep it TINY and the same size every time, because on a 2° grip a press that grows pushes the loft below zero and pace goes with it. Bend over MORE, stand CLOSE, eyes DOWN through the strike. ROUTINE: read and pick your spot from behind → step BESIDE the ball in full posture and take two rehearsals, eyes-on-ball then eyes-on-hole (the hole one is the PACE stroke — keep it last, and finish it with the press) → step in, face to the spot first, then stance → spot, ball, press, go. Grip settled: conventional / reverse-overlap.
sections.k: Ball off the left breast, weight stacked on it, shoulders rock — hands EVEN with the ball, press stays tiny.

rules: Driver: aim centre, swing LONGER not tighter
Mini driver: tee it LOW, weights back
Irons: trust the extra height, choke down to flight it
Putter: hands even, shoulders rock, no hands

entries.setup: ON COURSE · no film · Beekman scramble · L.A.B. DF3i (first round back) · greens estimated 8–9 stimp
entries.finding: The DF3i's first real evidence and it's good: pace felt dialled all day, a clutch 5-footer made on the 1st, and a 25-footer holed. Start line reported true on every putt — the first full round without the left miss showing up. Enough to settle the head; not yet enough to close either open fault, because the conditions were the friendliest available.
entries.detail:
Three things this DOES tell you. (1) START LINE: 'hitting my line all day' across a full round is the strongest counter-evidence yet to the fault measured 1.5–1.7° left on Jul 30 — and that measurement was taken on the LINK, a narrow blade with far less MOI and a riser hosel that hides where the head's centre really is. A heel strike closes a blade's face more than a mallet's. The left miss surviving three putters said it wasn't the equipment; a clean round on the mallet says at least some of it might have been. Re-measure overhead on the DF3i before crossing it off. (2) NERVE: a made 5-footer on the 1st is the routine working under the only pressure that counts. (3) The 25-footer is a bonus, not a data point — one long make is luck riding on decent pace.

And the caveat that matters most: 8–9 on the stimp is SLOW-to-medium (a well-kept public number; tour setups run 11–13). Slow greens flatter both open faults at once. You hit putts firmer, and firm takes break out — so a mediocre read still finds the hole and your line looks better than it is. And a slower surface is more forgiving of a strike that's off the middle, because you're swinging bigger to get there. Your pace calibration is now anchored to 8–9. On an 11 the same stroke runs four to six feet past from 30 feet. Log the speed with every lag ladder from here, and expect to recalibrate on quick greens rather than assuming this transfers.

faults.why: DOWNGRADED Aug 1 — first genuinely good news on this fault in the whole project. A full round on the DF3i with the line reported true on every putt, no left miss, and a 5-footer made under pressure on the 1st. That does not close it: the round was unmeasured, on 8–9 stimp greens where firmer putts take break out and flatter a mediocre read, and in a scramble where you often putt after seeing a teammate's ball. But it reopens a question worth asking — the 1.5–1.7° LEFT measured overhead on Jul 30 was measured on the LINK, a narrow blade that twists more on a heel strike and whose riser hosel makes the true centre hard to find by eye. The miss outliving three putters said it wasn't equipment; a clean round on the mallet says some of it might have been. Settle it the way it was raised: overhead, five putts, roll versus the mat centre line, on the DF3i. Median inside 0.5° and this comes off the card.

THE priority, and now it has its first evidence — with an asterisk. Pace felt dialled for a full round on the DF3i, which is exactly the thing that was missing when the head got benched on Jul 30 for lags coming up short. Worth noting how thin that verdict was: 12 days, no calibrated lag session, convicted on a feeling. The asterisk is green speed. Those greens were an estimated 8–9 on the stimp — slow-to-medium — so the curve you just built is anchored to a slow surface. The same stroke that finished perfectly there runs roughly four to six feet past from 30 feet on an 11. This is not calibration yet; it's one data point at one speed. 30-ft lag ladder twice a week: log spread, how many finish SHORT, and the green speed each time. Target no more than 1 in 10 short, and build the number on at least two different speeds before trusting it.

Still never measured, on any putter, not once — and the mallet lowers the stakes without removing them. A strike toward the HEEL rotates the face closed and starts the ball LEFT. That mattered more on the LINK: a narrow blade carries less MOI and twists more for the same distance off centre, and its riser hosel meant the shaft was a poor guide to where the mass sat. The DF3i is wide, deep and high-MOI, so the same miss costs less. That is now the leading explanation for why the left start line went quiet on Aug 1 — which makes measuring it MORE interesting, not less, because it would explain the whole pattern. Seven minutes: tap test to find the sweet spot, tape test to find the strike, compare.

Reopened by the grip reversion, and untouched by a round on the course. With the LINK's Pistol 0 there was no built-in lean to protect and the only question was repeatability. The DF3i's Press Pistol 2° supplies real lean at address, which brings back the old failure mode: a press added on top of it stacks loft off the bottom of the scale and drives the ball into the turf. A round that felt good doesn't test this — a driven ball still goes in from 5 feet, it just skids first and costs you on the long ones. One slo-mo face-on set — white tape on the shaft, 240 fps, lights on — compares lean at address with lean at impact and settles it.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓. At 120 fps and 37.5 px/inch the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of its address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames, and never dropped below address height. The rise afterwards is the follow-through arc. Measured on the LINK, but this is a stroke property rather than a head property — it should carry. Wants two more slo-mo strokes on sample size, and the next face-on set gives them for free.
CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — overhead film measured the toe line 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line across three reps. Never open.

metrics.name: Path
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — straight (SBST) across 20+ clips and four putters. Measured again Jul 30: ¼–½" inside at the top, back on the line by impact. Path is yours, not the putter's, which is why the head going back to the DF3i doesn't reopen it.

metrics.name: Tempo / load
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — 2.0:1 measured on the LINK.2.1, seven of eight clips between 1.9 and 2.1, two independent ways. Was 2.4:1 on the DF3i, which is the head now back in play. Both sit inside the window; stop checking this one.

metrics.name: Face at impact
metrics.verdict: REOPENED Jul 30 — zero-torque guarantees the face won't TWIST, and it doesn't. It cannot guarantee where the face POINTS, and on 2 of 3 measured putts it pointed ~1.5° left at impact. Aimed there or closed through: only a face-on clip separates them, and that clip is now owed on the DF3i.

metrics.name: Early lift
metrics.verdict: CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames. The oldest open item on the card, finally shut. It's a stroke property, not a head property, so it carries back to the mallet — but take two more slo-mo strokes on sample size.

metrics.name: Start line / aim
metrics.verdict: THE FAULT — but softening. Measured 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts Jul 30 (1.3–1.4" at 4 ft, ~2" at 6 ft), one dead straight. Then a full round on the DF3i Aug 1 with the line true all day and no left miss. Unmeasured and on slow greens, so it isn't closed — but note the overhead measurement was taken on the LINK's narrow blade, which twists more on a heel strike. Re-measure overhead on the mallet: median inside 0.5° and this comes off the card.

metrics.name: Stance line
metrics.verdict: NEW and CLOSED on arrival. Measured off the overhead frames: the toe line ran 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line — never open on any rep. The trail-foot creep is fixed. Look higher for the aim leak.

entries.text: PUTTING — The 30-ft LAG LADDER, twice a week, on the DF3i: 10 balls, log the SPREAD of stopping points, how many finish SHORT, and THE GREEN SPEED (or the surface — that mat, this practice green). Target no more than 1 in 10 short. The speed field is the new part and it matters: Aug 1 went well on greens estimated 8–9 stimp, which is slow-to-medium, so the curve you just built is anchored there. Build it on at least two different speeds before you trust it on a quick course.

briefing.focus: Aug 1, Beekman scramble. The DF3i went back in and delivered: pace dialled all day, a clutch 5-footer made on the 1st, a 25-footer holed, and the line true on every putt. The gate closes early in the mallet's favour — the DF3i is the putter going forward and the LINK.2.1 goes to storage. This plan is the record of what got decided, the one setup change that comes back with it, what the round does and doesn't prove, and the two things left to do before the decision is actually finished.
rules: The DF3i is the putter — the head is settled, stop shopping
The LINK didn't fail; it lost on redundancy
Press Pistol 2° is back: hands EVEN with the ball, press stays tiny
Your pace is calibrated to 8–9 stimp — log the speed, expect to recalibrate
Find the LINK's return window before it lapses

sections.t: What actually got decided
sections.k: The right head, and now with real evidence behind it — just evidence from friendly conditions.
sections.b:
The scramble was the DF3i's first round back and it delivered on the two things that were open: pace felt dialled all day, and the line was true on every putt. Add a clutch 5-footer made on the 1st and a 25-footer holed. That settles which head goes in the bag, and it's a good landing — you're back on the putter you've rolled your best with, it's still zero-torque, and the SBST mismatch that started this entire saga stays buried.

Be clear-eyed about what that evidence is, though, because being clear-eyed is what was missing when the DF3i got benched twelve days ago on an equally thin read. It's one round, unmeasured, in a scramble — where you're often putting after a teammate has already shown you the line and the pace — on greens you put at 8–9 on the stimp. That is the friendliest putting environment that exists. It doesn't make the decision wrong. It means the decision is right and the FAULTS aren't closed, which are two different things that are easy to collapse into one.

sections.t: The LINK didn't fail — worth saying plainly
sections.k: It lost on redundancy, not performance. Two zero-torque L.A.B. putters do one job.
sections.b:
Nothing on your card convicts the LINK.2.1. It produced the best measured numbers of the whole project: tempo 2.0:1 across seven of eight clips, an address position repeating to a third of a degree over 59 frames, a stance line measured square, and early lift closed for the first time since Session 1. What it never got was a pace baseline — the same thing the DF3i never got.

So your read is the right one, and it's the honest version: you like the putter, and you shouldn't own two. That's a redundancy call, not a performance call. Keeping both would mean two heads, two power curves, and a live temptation to switch every time a short one lipped out — which is precisely the loop that produced three putters in a month.

sections.t: What the round did to the left miss
sections.k: First clean round in the whole saga — and the Jul 30 measurement was taken on the blade, which is worth a second look.
sections.b:
The left miss on short putts is the through-line of this entire project, and Aug 1 is the first full round it didn't show up. That's worth something on its own.

It's also worth a question nobody has asked yet. The hard measurement — 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts — was taken on Jul 30, on the LINK. A narrow blade carries less MOI than a mallet, so a strike toward the heel twists the face closed MORE for the same distance off centre, and the LINK's riser hosel means the shaft isn't a reliable pointer to where the head's mass actually sits. Meanwhile strike location has never been measured on any putter you own.

The standing conclusion has been 'not equipment, because it survived three putters.' That still holds for the history. But a clean round on a high-MOI mallet is exactly what you'd expect if part of the Jul 30 number was the blade punishing a heel strike. Two tests settle it and both are cheap: re-measure overhead on the DF3i (five putts, roll versus the mat centre line, median inside 0.5°), and run the tape test to see where you're actually hitting it. Don't cross the fault off on the strength of a good afternoon — measure it off.

sections.t: The grip change comes back with it
sections.k: Press Pistol 2° means hands EVEN with the ball again — the vertical-shaft geometry was the LINK's, not yours.
sections.b:
This is the one thing that quietly changes your setup, and it's easy to miss because it looks like nothing.

The LINK ships with a L.A.B. Pistol 0 — zero built-in press — and the Jul 30 film measured exactly what that produces: a dead vertical shaft at address with your hands about 1.35" BEHIND the ball. Correct geometry for that putter, and the routine plan was rewritten around it.

The DF3i carries the Press Pistol 2°, and that grip leans the shaft for you. So the cue reverts: HANDS EVEN with the ball, and the grip supplies the lean. Do not carry the 'hands over the clubhead' feel across — on this grip it would be lean on top of lean.

And the rule that travelled with it is live again: keep any forward press genuinely TINY. With 2° already built in, a firm press pushes effective loft off the bottom of the scale and drives the ball into the turf. On the Pistol 0 there was no lean to double-count and that warning relaxed. On the DF3i it doesn't.

sections.t: What the mallet gives you back
sections.k: High MOI means an off-centre strike costs less — the strike question drops down the list, it doesn't disappear.
sections.b:
The DF3i is a wide, deep, high-MOI mallet; the LINK.2.1 is a narrow blade. In practice that means an off-centre strike on the mallet bleeds less ball speed and twists the head less than the same miss on the blade. That takes real pressure off the strike-location question that opened on Jul 30.

It does not close it. A heel strike still closes the face and still starts the ball left, which is still your signature miss, and strike location has never once been measured on any putter you own. The tap test and the tape test are seven minutes. Run them on the mallet.

The flip side is the honest cost of the swap: a blade REPORTS a bad strike where a mallet muffles it. The DF3i is more forgiving and less informative. That raises the value of measuring rather than feeling — which, given how this month has gone, is the theme.

sections.t: The one thing that has to happen this time
sections.k: One good round at one green speed isn't a power curve. Build it, and log the speed.
sections.b:
The DF3i was convicted on Jul 30 for lags coming up short and short putts running hot. That is not two faults — it's one power curve you hadn't learned, so you under-hit the long ones and over-hit the short ones. And it got convicted without a single calibrated lag session.

Aug 1 is the first evidence in the other direction and it's genuinely encouraging. It is also one round at one speed. Those greens ran an estimated 8–9 on the stimp, which is slow-to-medium — a well-kept public number, where tour setups run 11 to 13. Slow greens flatter you twice over: you swing bigger, which forgives a strike that's off the middle, and you hit putts firmer, and firm takes the break out, so a mediocre read still finds the hole. Your line looking perfect all day is partly the greens doing it for you.

So the standing item, twice a week: 10 balls from 30 feet, log the SPREAD of the stopping points, how many finish SHORT, and the GREEN SPEED. Target no more than 1 in 10 short. And build the curve at more than one speed — the stroke that finished perfectly at Beekman runs four to six feet past from 30 feet on an 11.

sections.t: Before the window closes
sections.k: Find the receipt and the deadline, then decide keep-or-return on purpose.
sections.b:
You're leaning return, and the reasoning holds. Make it a decision rather than a lapse: find the receipt, confirm the return window, and put the date somewhere you will actually see it.

If it goes back, the Pistol 0 goes with it. If the window has already closed the answer changes on its own — you keep it, it sits in storage as the control, and you don't game it.

One caution either way: don't clear the shelf to make room. The Newport 2 is the bullpen blade and the DF3i is the gamer; one spare is enough, and that slot is already filled.

sections.t: Stop shopping — the version that applies now
sections.k: The head is settled. From here the next thing that changes should be a number, not a putter.
sections.b:
The line from the routine plan, updated for where you actually are: that was three putters in a month, and the head has now settled on the one you've putted best with. The rule from here is simple — the next thing that changes is a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.

Path: settled. Tempo: settled. Stance line: square. Early lift: closed. What's open is start line and pace, and neither of those has ever been a shopping problem.

club.note: IN STORAGE from Aug 1 — out of the bag after the DF3i's scramble. CORRECTED Aug 2: an earlier note here said this head 'produced the best measured numbers of the whole project.' That was wrong and the grid says so — the LINK's column is the only one carrying TWO reds (face at impact, start line), and the DF3i's first filmed column carries none. What's true is narrower: individual metrics posted their best values on it (tempo 2.0:1 against the DF3i's 2.4:1, address repeating to 0.3° over 59 frames), and early lift and stance line were closed during its fortnight — but those two are stroke properties, and Jul 30 was simply the most heavily filmed day of the project, so that's measurement effort rather than a putter effect. Honest read: the numbers on this head are ambiguous, not favourable, and it never got a lag ladder or a 10-ball test either. It goes to storage on REDUNDANCY — two zero-torque L.A.B. putters do one job — which is a reason that holds however the numbers are read. LIKELY RETURNING: find the receipt, confirm the window before it lapses. If it goes back, the Pistol 0 grip goes with it.

briefing.focus: Aug 1, Beekman scramble. The DF3i went back in and delivered: pace dialled all day, a clutch 5-footer made on the 1st, a 25-footer holed, and the line true on every putt. The gate closes early in the mallet's favour — the DF3i is the putter going forward and the LINK.2.1 goes to storage. This plan is the record of what got decided, the one setup change that comes back with it, what the round does and doesn't prove, and the two things left to do before the decision is actually finished.
rules: The DF3i is the putter — the head is settled, stop shopping
The LINK didn't fail; it lost on redundancy
Press Pistol 2° is back: hands EVEN with the ball, press stays tiny
Your pace is calibrated to 8–9 stimp — log the speed, expect to recalibrate
Find the LINK's return window before it lapses

sections.t: What actually got decided
sections.k: The right head, and now with real evidence behind it — just evidence from friendly conditions.
sections.b:
The scramble was the DF3i's first round back and it delivered on the two things that were open: pace felt dialled all day, and the line was true on every putt. Add a clutch 5-footer made on the 1st and a 25-footer holed. That settles which head goes in the bag, and it's a good landing — you're back on the putter you've rolled your best with, it's still zero-torque, and the SBST mismatch that started this entire saga stays buried.

Be clear-eyed about what that evidence is, though, because being clear-eyed is what was missing when the DF3i got benched twelve days ago on an equally thin read. It's one round, unmeasured, in a scramble — where you're often putting after a teammate has already shown you the line and the pace — on greens you put at 8–9 on the stimp. That is the friendliest putting environment that exists. It doesn't make the decision wrong. It means the decision is right and the FAULTS aren't closed, which are two different things that are easy to collapse into one.

sections.t: What the LINK's numbers actually say
sections.k: Ambiguous, not favourable — its column carries the only two reds on the grid. It goes on redundancy, which holds either way.
sections.b:
CORRECTED Aug 2. An earlier version of this plan said the LINK.2.1 'produced the best measured numbers of the whole project' and that nothing on the card convicted it. That was too generous, and the evolution grid contradicts it directly: the LINK's column is the ONLY one carrying two reds — face at impact and start line — and the DF3i's first filmed column carries none. The single hard red on your card, the 1.5–1.7° left start line, was measured on the LINK.

The narrower true version: some individual metrics did post their best values during its fortnight. Tempo came in at 2.0:1 across seven of eight clips against the DF3i's 2.4:1, and 2:1 is the target. Address repeatability measured 0.3° over 59 frames. Early lift and stance line both got closed. But the last two are properties of your stroke rather than the head, and the reason they closed on Jul 30 is that Jul 30 was by far the most filmed day of this project — three sessions, fourteen clips, the first face-on at 120 fps. That is measurement effort, not a putter effect. Read fairly, the LINK's numbers are AMBIGUOUS, not favourable.

What genuinely holds is that it was never properly tested either — no lag ladder, no 10-ball test, the same gap that got the DF3i benched. So neither head has a real scoreboard, and the only one that exists is the DF3i's 8/10 from four feet on Jul 20.

None of which changes the decision, and that's the point worth keeping: it goes to storage on REDUNDANCY. You like the putter and you shouldn't own two zero-torque L.A.B. heads. That reason stands however the numbers are read, which is exactly why it's the right reason to decide on.

sections.t: What the round did to the left miss
sections.k: First clean round in the whole saga — and the Jul 30 measurement was taken on the blade, which is worth a second look.
sections.b:
The left miss on short putts is the through-line of this entire project, and Aug 1 is the first full round it didn't show up. That's worth something on its own.

It's also worth a question nobody has asked yet. The hard measurement — 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts — was taken on Jul 30, on the LINK. A narrow blade carries less MOI than a mallet, so a strike toward the heel twists the face closed MORE for the same distance off centre, and the LINK's riser hosel means the shaft isn't a reliable pointer to where the head's mass actually sits. Meanwhile strike location has never been measured on any putter you own.

The standing conclusion has been 'not equipment, because it survived three putters.' That still holds for the history. But a clean round on a high-MOI mallet is exactly what you'd expect if part of the Jul 30 number was the blade punishing a heel strike. Two tests settle it and both are cheap: re-measure overhead on the DF3i (five putts, roll versus the mat centre line, median inside 0.5°), and run the tape test to see where you're actually hitting it. Don't cross the fault off on the strength of a good afternoon — measure it off.

sections.t: The grip change comes back with it
sections.k: Press Pistol 2° means hands EVEN with the ball again — the vertical-shaft geometry was the LINK's, not yours.
sections.b:
This is the one thing that quietly changes your setup, and it's easy to miss because it looks like nothing.

The LINK ships with a L.A.B. Pistol 0 — zero built-in press — and the Jul 30 film measured exactly what that produces: a dead vertical shaft at address with your hands about 1.35" BEHIND the ball. Correct geometry for that putter, and the routine plan was rewritten around it.

The DF3i carries the Press Pistol 2°, and that grip leans the shaft for you. So the cue reverts: HANDS EVEN with the ball, and the grip supplies the lean. Do not carry the 'hands over the clubhead' feel across — on this grip it would be lean on top of lean.

And the rule that travelled with it is live again: keep any forward press genuinely TINY. With 2° already built in, a firm press pushes effective loft off the bottom of the scale and drives the ball into the turf. On the Pistol 0 there was no lean to double-count and that warning relaxed. On the DF3i it doesn't.

sections.t: What the mallet gives you back
sections.k: High MOI means an off-centre strike costs less — the strike question drops down the list, it doesn't disappear.
sections.b:
The DF3i is a wide, deep, high-MOI mallet; the LINK.2.1 is a narrow blade. In practice that means an off-centre strike on the mallet bleeds less ball speed and twists the head less than the same miss on the blade. That takes real pressure off the strike-location question that opened on Jul 30.

It does not close it. A heel strike still closes the face and still starts the ball left, which is still your signature miss, and strike location has never once been measured on any putter you own. The tap test and the tape test are seven minutes. Run them on the mallet.

The flip side is the honest cost of the swap: a blade REPORTS a bad strike where a mallet muffles it. The DF3i is more forgiving and less informative. That raises the value of measuring rather than feeling — which, given how this month has gone, is the theme.

sections.t: The one thing that has to happen this time
sections.k: One good round at one green speed isn't a power curve. Build it, and log the speed.
sections.b:
The DF3i was convicted on Jul 30 for lags coming up short and short putts running hot. That is not two faults — it's one power curve you hadn't learned, so you under-hit the long ones and over-hit the short ones. And it got convicted without a single calibrated lag session.

Aug 1 is the first evidence in the other direction and it's genuinely encouraging. It is also one round at one speed. Those greens ran an estimated 8–9 on the stimp, which is slow-to-medium — a well-kept public number, where tour setups run 11 to 13. Slow greens flatter you twice over: you swing bigger, which forgives a strike that's off the middle, and you hit putts firmer, and firm takes the break out, so a mediocre read still finds the hole. Your line looking perfect all day is partly the greens doing it for you.

So the standing item, twice a week: 10 balls from 30 feet, log the SPREAD of the stopping points, how many finish SHORT, and the GREEN SPEED. Target no more than 1 in 10 short. And build the curve at more than one speed — the stroke that finished perfectly at Beekman runs four to six feet past from 30 feet on an 11.

sections.t: Before the window closes
sections.k: Find the receipt and the deadline, then decide keep-or-return on purpose.
sections.b:
You're leaning return, and the reasoning holds. Make it a decision rather than a lapse: find the receipt, confirm the return window, and put the date somewhere you will actually see it.

If it goes back, the Pistol 0 goes with it. If the window has already closed the answer changes on its own — you keep it, it sits in storage as the control, and you don't game it.

One caution either way: don't clear the shelf to make room. The Newport 2 is the bullpen blade and the DF3i is the gamer; one spare is enough, and that slot is already filled.

sections.t: Stop shopping — the version that applies now
sections.k: The head is settled. From here the next thing that changes should be a number, not a putter.
sections.b:
The line from the routine plan, updated for where you actually are: that was three putters in a month, and the head has now settled on the one you've putted best with. The rule from here is simple — the next thing that changes is a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.

Path: settled. Tempo: settled. Stance line: square. Early lift: closed. What's open is start line and pace, and neither of those has ever been a shopping problem.

briefing.course: The Tape Test — Where You Actually Hit It
briefing.focus: Twelve minutes, at home, on the DF3i. Strike location is the last cheap thing on your card that has NEVER been measured — not on this putter, not on any putter you own — and it is the one candidate that could explain BOTH open faults at once. Two tests: a tap test to find the true sweet spot, then a marked face over 20 putts to find where you actually hit it. Photograph both and log the result.
rules: Find the sweet spot FIRST — you can't read a strike pattern without it
20 putts total: 10 from 5 ft, 10 from 30 ft — stroke length changes the pattern
Don't wipe between putts; the accumulated cluster IS the data
Photograph square-on, in good light, with the sweet-spot mark visible
Read the cluster's CENTRE, not its worst outlier
steps: TAP TEST — hold the putter loosely by the very top of the grip so it hangs free. Tap the face heel-to-toe with a pencil eraser. Where it swings straight back with NO twist is the true sweet spot.
Mark that spot with a sliver of tape on the TOPLINE, and photograph it next to the putter's sight line. Note whether they agree.
Coat the face — foot-powder spray is best (Dr. Scholl's or similar), dry-erase marker second. Light, even coat.
10 putts from 5 ft, full routine on each. Do not wipe the face.
Photograph the face square-on, then re-coat.
10 putts from 30 ft — the lag stroke. Photograph again.
Log it: put the two photos and a one-line read in the Putting Lab.

sections.t: Why this is the test worth running now
sections.k: One heel bias would explain the left start line AND the short lags — two faults, one root cause.
sections.b:
Here is the hypothesis this test is built to kill or confirm, and it's the most interesting idea on your card right now.

A strike toward the HEEL does two things at once. It rotates the face closed at impact, which starts the ball LEFT. And it bleeds ball speed, because you've missed the middle, which makes putts finish SHORT.

Now look at what you've actually complained about. On the DF3i, Jul 29: lags coming up short. On the LINK, Jul 30: the ball starting 1.5–1.7° left. Two different faults on two different putters — or one heel bias showing up differently on each head. The DF3i is a wide, high-MOI mallet: it resists the twist, so a heel strike costs you mostly SPEED. The LINK is a narrow blade with far less MOI: the same strike twists it more, so it costs you mostly DIRECTION.

That is a single root cause producing exactly the two symptoms you reported, on exactly the heads you reported them on. It might be wrong. But it's testable in twelve minutes, and nothing else on the card explains both.

sections.t: The tap test — find the sweet spot before you read anything
sections.k: Hang it from the grip and tap heel-to-toe; the spot with no twist is the real centre. Check it against the sight line.
sections.b:
You cannot read a strike pattern without knowing what you're reading it against, and the putter's SIGHT LINE is not automatically the answer.

Hold the putter loosely by the very top of the grip and let it hang. Tap the face with a pencil eraser, working heel to toe. Most taps make the head twist. One spot makes it swing straight back with no rotation at all — that's the sweet spot, and it's a physical property of the head, not a decoration on the topline. Mark it with a sliver of tape.

Then check it against the sight line. On the DF3i — a mallet with the shaft entering near the middle — I'd expect them to agree closely. This mattered far more on the LINK, where a heel-entry shaft is made lie-angle-balanced by a riser hosel, and L.A.B.'s own explanation says the shaft base points at a spot that is not necessarily the centre of gravity. If the DF3i's sweet spot and sight line DO agree, that's one less variable and worth knowing for certain rather than assuming.

sections.t: Marking the face — what to use
sections.k: Foot-powder spray is the right tool: no thickness, clean marks, wipes off.
sections.b:
FOOT-POWDER SPRAY (Dr. Scholl's or any odour spray) is the best option and the one to buy if you don't have it. It leaves a thin white coat, the ball wipes a clean mark, it adds no thickness, and it comes off with a cloth.

DRY-ERASE MARKER works nearly as well — colour the face, the ball lifts the ink off where it touches.

BABY POWDER over a lightly damp face is the free version and it's fussier but fine.

What to avoid: thick impact TAPE. It's designed for this, but it adds a layer between face and ball, which changes both the sound and the roll slightly. For finding a cluster that's tolerable; for anything you also want to feel, it isn't. And don't use anything on the BALL — you want the mark on the face, where the sweet spot is.

sections.t: Do it at both lengths — this is the part people skip
sections.k: Short-putt and lag strokes can strike differently, and each maps to a different fault.
sections.b:
10 from 5 feet and 10 from 30 feet, photographed separately. This matters more than it sounds.

A short-putt stroke and a lag stroke are different motions — different length, different speed, different amount of body in it. Strike patterns often differ between them, and in your case the two lengths map onto the two different faults. The 5-footers are where the LEFT MISS lives. The 30-footers are where the SHORT LAGS live.

If the heel bias shows up at both lengths, it's a setup fault — where you're standing, where your eyes are. If it only shows up on the long stroke, it's a motion fault that appears when the stroke gets big. Those have different fixes, and one photo of one length can't tell them apart.

sections.t: How to read the two photos
sections.k: Read the cluster's centre against your tape mark — bias tells you the fault, scatter tells you a different one.
sections.b:
Look at where the CENTRE of the cluster sits relative to the tape mark, and separately at how tight the cluster is. They answer different questions.

TIGHT CLUSTER ON THE MARK — strike location is not your problem. Cross it off, and the left start line is down to aim or face-at-impact, which is what the face-on clip settles. That's a clean, useful result: it eliminates the cheapest candidate and puts everything on the one clip you already owe.

CLUSTER BIASED TOWARD THE HEEL — the hypothesis is live, and you've found something that explains both faults at once.

CLUSTER BIASED TOWARD THE TOE — real too, and it pushes the ball the other way (toe strike opens the face, starts it right). That would NOT explain a left miss, so it'd mean the left miss is aim or face and you've found a separate pace leak.

WIDE SCATTER, NO BIAS — that's a different fault with a different name: not a strike bias but strike CONSISTENCY, and it usually traces to a distance-from-the-ball that varies, or eye line drifting. Also worth knowing, also fixable.

One honesty note on magnitude: how many degrees a given miss costs depends on the head's MOI, and I'm not going to hand you a degrees-per-inch number I can't stand behind for this specific putter. What the test gives you cleanly is DIRECTION and CONSISTENCY of the bias. That's enough to act on.

sections.t: If it comes back heel-biased
sections.k: Usually a setup cause — eye line inside the ball or standing too close. Change one thing, re-shoot.
sections.b:
Don't jump to the stroke. The usual causes are geometric and dull.

EYE LINE INSIDE THE BALL is the most common. Eyes set inside the target line tend to pull the strike toward the heel. Never measured on you — drop a ball from the bridge of your nose at address and see where it lands relative to the ball. That's a ten-second check and it belongs in the same session.

STANDING TOO CLOSE crowds the hands and brings the heel in.

SETUP FIX WORTH TRYING FIRST: address the ball off the CENTRE of the face deliberately — you may currently be setting up with the ball slightly toward the heel and delivering exactly what you aimed at.

Then re-shoot the test after the change. That's the whole loop, and it's fast: measure, change one thing, measure again. Ten more putts tells you whether the fix took.

sections.t: What this does and doesn't settle
sections.k: It removes or confirms a candidate. It doesn't replace the face-on clip.
sections.b:
Be clear about the scope so the result doesn't get over-read, because that's been the pattern this month.

What it settles: whether strike location is a live candidate for the left start line, and whether you have a hidden pace leak that no amount of tempo work would fix.

What it does NOT settle: where the face is POINTING. A perfectly centred strike with the face aimed 1.5° left produces the same miss and this test can't see it. The face-on clip is still owed and still the item that closes the most faults at once.

And it doesn't replace the lag ladder. Strike quality and pace calibration are different things — you can strike it perfectly and still not know how hard 30 feet is on an 11 stimp.

entries.text: PUTTING — RUN THE TAPE TEST on the DF3i (~12 min, at home). Full protocol is in the 'Tape Test — Where You Actually Hit It' plan. Short version: (1) hang the putter from the top of the grip and tap the face heel-to-toe with an eraser — the spot with NO twist is the true sweet spot, mark it with tape and check it against the sight line. (2) Coat the face with foot-powder spray, hit 10 from 5 ft, photograph; re-coat, hit 10 from 30 ft, photograph. Don't wipe between putts. This is the last cheap untested thing on your card and it's the only candidate that explains BOTH open faults — a heel strike closes the face (starts it LEFT) and bleeds ball speed (lags SHORT). Send the two photos.

club.note: KEPT — decided Aug 10. The return-window question is closed by decision rather than by expiry. This stays out of the 14 as the INDOOR / AWAY-FROM-THE-BAG PRACTICE PUTTER. Be honest about why: the training-specificity case for practising on the LINK does not hold — it points at the DF3i, which is its own best practice putter — and the blade-feedback case is answered for $8 of foot-powder spray on the gamer. What does hold is AVAILABILITY: a putter that lives inside collects more reps than one locked in the car, and reps actually taken beat better reps that aren't. Kept because it's liked and it'll get used, not because it trains anything the DF3i can't. ROLE SPLIT — LINK: motion and volume only (path, tempo, keeping the face passive). DF3i: anything carrying a measurement or a setup component — the alignment-tape work, the tap test, gate work, filmed sessions, pre-round reps. NOT BEING REGRIPPED: the Pistol 0 stays. Lie Angle Balance is a property of the assembled club, grip included, so a local-shop swap to a Press Pistol 2° risks putting the head out of spec with no way to verify it. If they're ever to be matched, that's a job for L.A.B. themselves. GUARD: the two grips ask for different hand positions — Pistol 0 sets the hands ~1.35" behind the ball, the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° sets them even with it — so don't go straight from LINK reps into a round or a filmed DF3i set. Roll a handful on the DF3i first to reset the hands. WATCH: Jul 30 measured tempo at 2.0:1 on the LINK against 2.4:1 on the DF3i, so transfer between the two heads is NOT proven. If the LINK becomes a regular tool, film one DF3i set before and after a LINK session and confirm it isn't dragging the gamer's tempo around.

entries.text: L.A.B. LINK.2.1 KEPT, not returned — settled Aug 10 by decision rather than by the window lapsing. Stays out of the 14 as the indoor practice putter, on availability rather than any training advantage over the DF3i. Pistol 0 grip stays with it: no regrip, since Lie Angle Balance includes the grip.

entries.setup: 23 clips · 120 fps slo-mo · outdoor practice green, 14:26–14:58 · L.A.B. DF3i (10 clips, 2 sets) + LINK.2.1 (13 clips, 3 sets) · five ground-level camera positions — front-quarter and rear-quarter, none overhead, none square face-on
entries.finding: First outdoor film since the LINK was kept, and the pace news is genuinely good: on the two long putts where the ball, the cup and the whole roll are all in frame — one DF3i at 14:45, one LINK at 14:49 — the ball came to rest 2–4 INCHES from the hole. Dead-weight lags on a real green, which is exactly the evidence the pace card has been short of since Beekman. The diagnostic news is that none of the five camera positions is one of the two angles you owe. Every clip is ground-level and oblique, so start line, face and shaft lean all stay exactly where they were — and be careful reading these back yourself: the shaft LOOKS leaned away from the target in every clip, including clips where the putt goes the other way, which is projection from a low side-on camera, not a position. Third thing, and it matters for the comparison you were trying to run: the two putters never played the same putt. DF3i took the first two sets, LINK the last three, different holes and different lengths, so nothing here compares the heads.

metrics.n: 2 sets vs 3 sets, never the same putt

detail.story:
WHAT WAS SHOT. Twenty-three clips over thirty-two minutes on the practice green, all 120 fps, in five sets that each moved the camera. The heads alternate: DF3i for the first six clips (14:26–14:46) and again at 14:51, LINK.2.1 at 14:48–14:49, 14:53–14:55 and 14:56–14:58. That's ten clips on the gamer and thirteen on the backup, and it means the session finished on the LINK — nine clips, the last seven minutes, and the shortest putts of the day.

THE GOOD NEWS IS PACE. Two putts could be measured properly, because the ball, the cup and the entire roll all stayed in one frame: the 14:45 DF3i putt and the 14:49 LINK putt, both long — 20-plus feet by eye. Both finished 2–4 inches from the cup, measured against the ball's own diameter at rest, which is the one scale in a golf video you can always trust. Neither went in. Both were the dead-weight speed that leaves a tap-in. That is the first pace evidence on a real green since Beekman, and unlike Beekman it is measured rather than remembered.

WHAT THE STROKE TRACES SHOW. Two clips — one on each head — gave a clean enough read on the head through the stroke to time the parts: the DF3i clip ran about 0.40 s back and 0.20 s down, the LINK about 0.52 s back and 0.28 s down. Both land inside the 1.9–2.1 window that got tempo marked SETTLED, and both peak in head speed at the ball rather than before it. So nothing in today's film says the LINK is dragging the gamer's tempo around, which was the explicit worry when it was kept eight hours ago. Two clips is not a verdict — that watch item stays open — but it points the right way.

THE PROBLEM IS THE ANGLES. Five camera positions and not one of them is square to anything. Every clip sits low and oblique — either in front of you and off to the side, or behind you and off to the side. That view can see roll, pace and the timing of the stroke, and it does. It cannot see where the face points, how far the ball starts off line, or where the hands sit relative to the ball, and no amount of frame-by-frame work on this footage changes that.

ONE TRAP WORTH NAMING. In these clips the shaft appears to lean AWAY from the target at address. It appears that way in clips where the putt runs left across the frame and in clips where it runs right — which is the giveaway. A low camera off to one side projects a shaft that leans toward or away from it onto the image the same way regardless of which way the putt is aimed. If you scrub these back on your phone and read hands-behind-the-ball off them, you'll be reading the lens. That question is still only answerable from square-on, and it is still open.
detail.compare:
Every measured angle before this was indoors on the mat; this is the first film outdoors. That is a real gain and a real loss at once.

THE GAIN: green speed and roll-out are things a mat cannot show you at all, and the two tracked putts give the pace card its first measured outdoor point. Jul 30 gave path, tempo and early-lift, all indoors, none of which needed a green. Aug 1 at Beekman gave pace, on a green, but by feel and with no camera. Today is the first time those two halves have overlapped — measured, on grass.

THE LOSS: the mat gave a straight reference line to measure start line against, controlled light, and a camera you could square up and leave. Outdoors you got sunshine, a moving handheld camera and five positions in thirty-two minutes, none of them repeated exactly. The Jul 30 overhead measured 1.5–1.7° left because there was a printed line to measure against. There is nothing to measure against here.

ON THE HEAD-TO-HEAD: the alternating sets look like an A/B and aren't one. The DF3i took the long putts from the far side of the green in the first half, the LINK took the short ones from close range at the end. Different lengths, different holes, different camera. To compare the heads you have to alternate them ball-for-ball from the SAME spot to the SAME hole — five with one, five with the other, then swap back — or the comparison measures the putt, not the putter.
detail.limits:
This set cannot close a single open item on the card, and it is worth being precise about why.

START LINE needs the ball's first two feet of roll measured against a known straight line, from above. No clip here is overhead, and there is no reference line on a practice green. Not answerable.

FACE AT IMPACT needs the camera square to the target line at ball height. Every clip is oblique. Not answerable.

SHAFT LEAN needs the same square angle plus white tape on the shaft at 240 fps — that was the prescription after Jul 30, and the tape still isn't on the shaft. Not answerable, and actively misleading from this angle, as above.

STRIKE LOCATION needs foot-powder spray on the face, not video. Still never measured on any putter.

PACE is the one that moved, and even there, two putts is two putts. The lag ladder asks for ten balls from 30 ft with the SPREAD and the green speed logged; what you have is two long putts that both finished stone dead. Encouraging, not calibration — and note that both of them finished a couple of inches SHORT of the cup rather than past it, which is the direction this fault has always leaned.

entries.text: PUTTING — ONE FACE-ON CLIP. Still the only thing standing between you and a diagnosis: it separates 'face aimed left' from 'face closing through impact', closes the held-press question (lean at address vs at impact) and confirms early-lift. NOT TICKED BY AUG 10 — that session ran 23 clips from five camera positions and every one of them was oblique, which is why it read pace beautifully and settled nothing else. The spec is narrow on purpose: camera at BALL HEIGHT, square to the target line (stand it behind the ball, walk to a spot 90° off the line, phone on the ground), white tape on the shaft ~6" above the head, 240 fps, 2–3 strokes, on the DF3i. Do it indoors if that's what it takes to get the camera square and left alone — this clip does not need a green. One good clip beats twenty from the wrong angle.

entries.setup: 23 clips · 120 fps slo-mo · outdoor practice green with ABOVE-GROUND cups, 14:26–14:58 · L.A.B. DF3i (10 clips) + LINK.2.1 (13 clips) · five ground-level camera positions · two balls per rep (one blue, one white)
entries.finding: Re-scored the whole session once the key fact about this green was in: the cups are above-ground bases, so the ball can never drop — which means the FINAL FRAME OF EVERY CLIP shows the true outcome, and the session went from two measurable putts to seventeen. The scoring is lopsided in the right direction: 7 putts finished DEAD — touching the base or inside ~6 inches — another ~5 inside a foot and a half, and the worst putt of the entire day was about 4 feet. Nothing raced past; no ricochets off the base; every arrival that could be tracked came in at dying speed. Both heads posted dead finishes: DF3i from long range and from 5 feet, LINK from long range and repeatedly from 6–8 feet, including three of the last four putts of the day parked against the base. The left-miss story gets nothing here — the camera angles still can't score direction against a line — but as a PACE session this is the best evidence yet, and it's measured, not remembered. One oddity worth answering: in all five closing clips the WHITE ball dies at the base and the BLUE ball finishes 1.2–1.5 ft away on the same side, five times in a row — deliberate second target, or is that ball doing something?

metrics.n: one, set D · zero blow-bys all day
no overhead, no square face-on — direction unscored

detail.story:
WHY THE RE-SCORE. These cups sit ON the green, not in it. A ball can't disappear, so the last frame of every clip is a scorecard — and that turns a 23-clip session shot from diagnostic-useless angles into a seventeen-putt pace ledger. All distances below were measured against the ball's own diameter at rest (1.68"), the one scale in a golf video that can't lie.

THE LEDGER, SET BY SET. Set A — DF3i, 14:26–14:47, medium-to-long range, five camera-visible finishes: one long putt rolled the width of the green and stopped touching the base; a second finished dead against it from mid-range; one rep left both balls 2.5–3.5 ft short; one putt never reached the two-foot circle; one finished about a foot away. Set B — LINK, 14:48–14:49, the long right-to-left putt tracked ball-to-rest arrived at dying speed and stopped AT the base, with a second ball sitting 4–6 inches off it a clip later. Set C — DF3i, 14:51, five-footers: blue dead against the base, the whites inside 8–14 inches, whole cluster inside 2.5 ft. Set D — LINK, ~20 ft: one dead (2–4 in), one ~2 ft, one ~3.5–4 ft — the day's worst. Set E — LINK, 14:56–14:58, 6–8 ft, the closing five clips: white dead at the base in clips 20, 22 and 23, white at ~5 in in 21, and the blue ball 1.2–1.5 ft off the base in every single one.

WHAT THE TALLY SAYS. 7 of 17 dead, ~12 of 17 inside a foot and a half, worst ~4 ft, ZERO long. For a player whose pace card carries 'lags come up short' as the open conviction, a day with no blow-bys reads at first like more of the same lean — but look at where the short ones died: the misses cluster AROUND the base, not three feet before it. This is what calibrated-but-conservative looks like, and on the two speeds now sampled (Beekman's 8–9 stimp and this practice green) the curve is holding.

THE HONEST CAVEATS. First: an above-ground base STOPS a ball that touches it. Some of those seven dead finishes would have trickled a foot or two past on a real green — the bases mask the long tail. The tracked arrivals came in soft, with no visible ricochet, so none of them were hot; but 'dead at the base' here means 'make-or-tap-in', not 'perfect dying weight', and the distinction matters for the lag-ladder numbers, where a base won't save you. Second: ball attribution. He collects balls between most clips, but where a ball may have carried over from the previous clip (the blue in set B), it's counted once, not twice. Third: direction is still unscored — these angles can't measure start line against anything, so left/right of the base in a given frame is camera geometry, not a miss pattern, and no left-miss conclusion is drawn from any of it.

THE BLUE-BALL QUESTION. Five closing clips, same result five times: white dies at the base, blue stops 1.2–1.5 ft off it, same side. Three explanations fit: the blue putt was aimed at a different spot on purpose; the blue is the first, feel-finding rep each time; or that ball behaves differently (a colored range-type ball can run differently off the face). If the blue was aimed at the same base — say so, because a repeating 1.5-ft error on one ball and none on the other is worth one foot-powder session on its own.
