Both cameras this evening were ON the line — excellent for start line, useless for shaft lean, because lean lives in the plane those cameras are looking down. So lean at address versus impact, the hands-behind-the-ball position the Pistol 0 wants, and ball position rep-to-rep are all still unmeasured. White tape on the shaft: still not on.

ALSO UNTOUCHED: strike location (foot-powder, still unrun) and pace — a 6-to-10-foot indoor mat cannot hold a 30-ft lag ladder, and distance control is the live priority and the reason the last putter went back.

entries.text: PUTTING — PUT A NUMBER ON 'BARELY OPEN'. PART-SERVED Aug 10 pm and the important half is still open. The mat clips gave the first start-line numbers since Jul 30 — one putt dead straight (inside 0.1" of the printed line), one about 1° left — which is better than Jul 30's 1.5–1.7° left but was measured on a mat WITH A PRINTED LINE. That line does the aiming for you, and 10/10 start lines on a mat is the one test you have always passed while the miss shows up on the course. So it does not test the aim hypothesis. TWO THINGS LEFT, both cheap. (1) VERIFY WITHOUT A LINE: five putts at a real target — a coin or a tee on the practice green, nothing drawn on the ground — filmed from directly behind the ball on the line. That is the test the mat cannot give you, and it is the one that decides whether 'barely open' is a genuine aim correction. (2) QUANTIFY THE FACE: the evening clips cannot measure it — the head is ~70 pixels wide and 1.5° is under two pixels — so shoot ONE close-up, phone directly above the ball, zoomed until the head fills the frame, face set at your new 'barely open', against a drawn line. Then re-check monthly, because an unquantified feel drifts toward the exaggeration. DON'T STACK FIXES: keep the feel and verify it, OR retrain the aim picture with a mirror — never both.

PUTTING — ONE FACE-ON CLIP, on the LINK.2.1. STILL NOT SHOT, and Aug 10 missed it twice in one day. The afternoon ran 23 clips from five positions, all oblique. The evening ran five clips from two positions, both ON the target line — genuinely the right angles for start line, and they delivered it, but lean lives in the plane those cameras look straight down, so they cannot see it. Face-on is now the ONLY angle you have never shot, and it is the only one left that can give you: shaft lean at ADDRESS versus at IMPACT on the Pistol 0 (expect ~0° at address, hands ~1.35" behind — the question is whether the press adds any), BALL POSITION rep to rep, which feeds the distance grind, and two more strokes of sample on the closed early-lift verdict. The spec is narrow on purpose: camera at BALL HEIGHT, square to the target line — stand it behind the ball, walk to a spot 90° off the line, phone on the ground — white tape on the shaft ~6" above the head, 240 fps, 2–3 strokes. Indoors is fine; this clip does not need a green. One good clip beats twenty from the wrong angle.

faults.why: FIRST MEASUREMENT SINCE JUL 30, and it moved the right way. Two putts filmed Aug 10 evening on an indoor lined mat, tracked against the printed centre line and scaled by the ball's own 1.68" diameter: one rolled dead straight (inside ~0.1" the whole way, about 0.8°, within the noise), the other started on the line and drifted about 1.0–1.3" LEFT by the hole, call it 1°. One square, one a degree left, no consistent bias — against a Jul 30 baseline of 1.5–1.7° LEFT on two of three. Encouraging. NOT CLOSED, for three reasons and the third is the one that matters. It is two putts at roughly ±0.5° uncertainty. Face angle itself was not measurable — the head spans ~70 pixels, where 1.5° is under two pixels — so nothing here confirms what 'barely open' actually is. And it was a MAT WITH A PRINTED LINE, which does the aiming for you: 10/10 start lines on a mat is the oldest line in this file, sitting alongside a miss that only ever appears on the course. The barely-open find is an explanation for exactly that split, so the test that decides it is five putts at a real target with NOTHING drawn on the ground, filmed from behind the ball. Until that exists, this fault is improving on the evidence available and untested where it actually lives.

THE priority, and it has a receipt: it cost you a putter. The DF3i went back Aug 10 because distance was too hard to control with it — after being benched for pace Jul 30, reprieved for pace Aug 1, and returned for pace Aug 10, three verdicts in eleven days without one calibrated lag session. The Aug 10 afternoon is the first real evidence in the other direction: ~20 putts scored off above-ground cups, NINE dead, worst ~4 ft, nothing long, and the short ones dying AROUND the base rather than feet before it — that is what calibrated-but-conservative looks like, on a second green speed. Still missing: a proper 30-ft ladder with shorts, spread and green speed logged, and the 20/30/40 set mapping distance to BACKSTROKE LENGTH at fixed tempo. Note the evening session could not touch this — a 6-to-10-foot indoor mat cannot hold a lag ladder, so the priority fault got no data from the clips that arrived. Tempo is not the missing piece: 2.0:1 on this head against a 2:1 target. Stroke length and strike are. And run the ladder with the gamer ball model only — the blue ball scattered to 1.2–1.5 ft on putts the white killed.

Still never measured on any putter, not once, across four heads — and now the biggest cheap thing left on the card. An off-centre hit bleeds ball speed, so the same stroke finishes short and the spread widens; a heel strike also rotates the face closed and starts the ball LEFT. One cause, both open faults. Two independent nudges from Aug 10 make it more interesting, not less: the blue-ball scatter (1.2–1.5 ft on putts the white ball killed from the same spot) has no aim explanation left, and the evening mat putts showed one straight roll and one drifting a degree left with no visible change in the stroke — which is what a strike moving around on the face looks like. The LINK punishes it harder than the mallet did: narrow blade, less MOI, and a riser hosel that makes the true centre impossible to find by eye. Twelve minutes — tap test for the sweet spot, foot-powder sheets from 5 ft and 30 ft, the 30-ft sheet being the one that matters. Run it with the new barely-open address, since that is the setup you will actually use.

Open, and Aug 10 could not touch it — twice. The afternoon's 23 clips were all oblique; the evening's five were all ON the target line, which is right for start line and blind to shaft lean, because lean lives in the plane those cameras look down. So face-on is now the only angle never shot. What it has to settle: the Press Pistol 2° went back with the DF3i, so the LINK's Pistol 0 supplies no lean at all — shaft vertical at address, hands ~1.35" behind the ball — and the soft press is now the ONLY lean in the stroke. The old 'don't double-count the lean' arithmetic is retired; what replaces it is consistency, because a press that varies is a launch that varies, which is a pace that varies, feeding straight into the priority fault. One slo-mo face-on set gives lean at address versus impact AND ball position rep to rep in the same clips. Whatever the tape shows IS the press now, with no built-in 2° to subtract.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓. At 120 fps and 37.5 px/inch the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of its address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames, and never dropped below address height. Measured on the LINK, which is the head still in play, so it carries cleanly. Wants two more slo-mo strokes on sample size — and the owed face-on set gives them for free, which is one more reason to shoot it.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — overhead film measured the toe line 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line across three reps. Never open. Worth re-reading in light of the Aug 10 find: this measurement is what ruled the feet out and sent the search higher, which is exactly where the face turned out to be.

metrics.name: Start line / aim
metrics.verdict: OPEN — but for the first time there is a candidate fix, found Aug 10: setting the face BARELY OPEN at address. The measured fault is 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts Jul 30 (1.3–1.4" at 4 ft, ~2" at 6 ft), one dead straight. Because a zero-torque head delivers the angle you set rather than twisting, a face pointing left at impact was pointing left at address — so this is an AIM error, and 'barely open' is you correcting it. Confirm the same way it was raised: overhead, five putts, new address, roll versus the mat centre line. Median inside 0.5° and this finally comes off the card. MEASURED AGAIN Aug 10 pm, first time since Jul 30: two putts on an indoor lined mat, tracked against the printed centre line — one dead straight (inside ~0.1", about 0.8°, within noise), one drifting about 1° LEFT by the hole. One square, one a degree left, no consistent bias, against a 1.5–1.7° left baseline. Real improvement, two big asterisks: n=2 at roughly ±0.5°, and a printed line does the aiming for you. The test that counts is five putts at a real target with nothing drawn on the ground.

metrics.name: Face at impact
metrics.verdict: REOPENED Jul 30, and Aug 10 supplies the likely answer. Zero-torque guarantees the face won't TWIST, and it doesn't. It cannot guarantee where the face POINTS, and on 2 of 3 measured putts it pointed ~1.5° left at impact. The two candidates were 'aimed there' and 'closed through' — and the barely-open find lands hard on AIMED THERE, since an address offset is exactly what a non-twisting head would carry to impact unchanged. Not confirmed until the overhead five says so, but this is no longer a coin flip. Aug 10 pm adds indirect evidence only. Start line is the best available proxy for face at impact on a putt, and it came back close to square on a lined mat. The face ITSELF was not measurable: the head spans ~70 pixels in those clips and 1.5° is under two pixels. A close-up from directly above the ball is what would put a number on 'barely open'.

metrics.name: Distance control
metrics.verdict: NEVER MEASURED — a full row of dashes, and that is the finding. Pace has now decided the fate of two putters and been quantified zero times: the DF3i was benched for it Jul 30, reprieved for it Aug 1, and RETURNED for it Aug 10. Every one of those calls was made on feel. This row fills in the moment the 30-ft ladder starts logging shorts, spread and green speed on the LINK. Until then, the most expensive fault on the card is also the only one with no data behind it.

metrics.name: Path
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — straight (SBST) across 20+ clips and four putters. Measured again Jul 30 on the LINK: ¼–½" inside at the top, back on the line by impact. Path is yours, not the putter's, which is why none of the head changes have reopened it — and why the left miss was never going to be explained by the stroke's shape.

metrics.name: Tempo / load
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — 2.0:1 measured on the LINK.2.1, seven of eight clips between 1.9 and 2.1, two independent ways, against a 2:1 target. It was 2.4:1 on the DF3i, but that head has gone back, so the number that counts is the one on the putter in the bag and it's the better of the two. Worth stating plainly for the pace grind: tempo is NOT your distance problem. Stroke length and strike are.

metrics.name: Early lift
metrics.verdict: CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames. The oldest open item on the card, finally shut, and measured on the head still in the bag. Take two more slo-mo strokes on sample size when the face-on set happens.

metrics.name: Stance line
metrics.verdict: CLOSED on arrival — the toe line ran 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line, never open on any rep. The trail-foot creep is fixed. This is the measurement that ruled the feet out and sent the search higher for the aim leak, and on Aug 10 that search found the face.

entries.setup: TWO BATCHES, ONE DAY. (1) AFTERNOON, 14:26–14:58 — 23 clips · 120 fps slo-mo · outdoor practice green with ABOVE-GROUND cups · L.A.B. DF3i (10 clips) + LINK.2.1 (13) · five ground-level camera positions, all oblique · two balls per rep (one blue, one white). (2) EVENING, ~19:54 — 6 clips, COMPLETE · indoor mat with a printed centre line · 3 putts on the LINK.2.1, each shot from TWO ANGLES, both ALONG the target line: down-the-line from floor level behind the ball (img0015 / img0016 / img0017) and reverse down-the-line from the hole end (IMG_3476 / img3477 / img3478), slow-motion. No face-on, no overhead.
entries.finding:
TWO SESSIONS, AND BETWEEN THEM THE FIRST FULL SET OF START-LINE NUMBERS SINCE JUL 30. Afternoon, outdoors: about 20 putts scored off above-ground cups — NINE dead (touching the base or inside ~6 inches), worst ~4 feet, nothing long, both heads posting dead finishes at every distance sampled. The blue-ball question closed with Jack's answer that both balls were aimed at the same base: the blue sat parked across three clips, so it took three putts not five, and all three finished 1.2–1.5 ft from the base on both sides while the white died on the same putts — so pace work runs with the gamer ball model only. Direction went unscored: all 23 clips were oblique.

EVENING, INDOORS — three putts, two angles each, both ON the target line, which is what finally made direction measurable. Tracked frame by frame against the mat's printed centre line, scaled by the ball's own 1.68" diameter at each depth; a stationary printed dash on that line reads 0.00" in every clip, which is what says the reference is unbiased. PUTT A: ~0.8° RIGHT (0.09" at the hole). PUTT B: ~1.0° LEFT (1.33"). PUTT C: started dead on the line, finished ~0.6° RIGHT (0.17"). Mean bias ≈0.1° right — zero. Median miss 0.8°.

THE SHAPE OF THE FAULT CHANGED, and that matters more than the improvement. Jul 30 was 1.5° LEFT, 1.7° LEFT and one straight: three putts pulling the same way, which is what an AIM error looks like, because aim does not change between reps. Tonight scatters either side of zero and the one-way pull did not reproduce once. The measured left miss is gone from these putts; DISPERSION is what replaced it. A bias points at aim — and the barely-open setup is the obvious candidate for having removed it. A two-way scatter points at something that varies stroke to stroke, and the leading candidate, never measured on any of the four putters owned this month, is STRIKE LOCATION: heel and toe contact rotate the face in opposite directions, which is a scatter with no bias. Inference, not measurement — the foot-powder test settles it in twelve minutes.

THREE CAVEATS THAT ALL STILL STAND. n=3, at roughly ±0.5° each, so the residual scatter is at the edge of what a phone on a mat can resolve — the absence of the bias is the robust finding, not the size of what's left. By the project's own gate, median inside 0.5°, this does NOT come off the card: 0.8° is better than 1.6° and it is not passed. And it was a MAT WITH A PRINTED LINE, which does the aiming for you — 10/10 start lines on a mat against a miss that only appears on the course is the oldest split in this file, and the barely-open find is an explanation for exactly that split. Face angle itself was not measurable in any clip: the head spans ~70 pixels, where 1.5° is under two pixels.

metrics.n: one, set D · zero long all day
same base target — white died on same putts
both cameras were ON the line

detail.story:
WHY THE RE-SCORE. These cups sit ON the green, not in it. A ball can't disappear, so the last frame of every clip is a scorecard — and that turned a session shot from diagnostic-useless angles into a ~20-putt pace ledger. Distances measured against the ball's own diameter at rest (1.68"), the one scale in a golf video that can't lie.

THE LEDGER, SET BY SET. Set A — DF3i, 14:26–14:47, medium-to-long: one long putt rolled the width of the green and stopped touching the base; a second finished dead from mid-range; one rep left both balls 2.5–3.5 ft short; one putt never reached the two-foot circle; one finished about a foot away. Set B — LINK, 14:48–14:49: the long right-to-left putt tracked ball-to-rest arrived at dying speed and stopped AT the base. Set C — DF3i, 14:51, five-footers: blue dead against the base, whites inside 8–14 inches, the whole cluster inside 2.5 ft. Set D — LINK, ~20 ft: one dead (2–4 in), one ~2 ft, one ~3.5–4 ft — the day's worst. Set E — LINK, 14:56–14:58, 6–8 ft: the white ball ran 2.3 ft, dead, 5 in, dead, dead across five putts; the blue took three putts and finished 1.2–1.5 ft every time.

WHAT THE TALLY SAYS. Nine of ~20 dead, most of the rest inside a foot and a half, worst ~4 ft, zero long. For a player whose pace card carries 'lags come up short' as the open conviction, the telling part is WHERE the short ones died: clustered around the base, not three feet before it. That is what calibrated-but-conservative looks like, and on the two speeds now sampled — Beekman's 8–9 stimp and this practice green — the curve is holding.

THE BLUE BALL, CLOSED AND REOPENED. The original oddity — 'blue finishes 1.2–1.5 ft in five straight finals' — was half camera artifact: frame-by-frame comparison shows the blue parked in the identical spot across clips 19–21, so it was putted three times, not five. The corrected fact is stranger: three blue putts, three finishes at 1.2–1.5 ft, spread across BOTH sides of the base, while the white died on the same putts from the same distance with the same putter. Jack confirms both were aimed at the same base, which rules out the easy explanation. Two remain. Small sample — three putts is three putts. Or the ball: a colored ball of a different model comes off the face at a different speed, and a repeating ~1.4 ft distance error at 7 feet is exactly what a firmer or softer cover does. Either way the operational rule is the same and it's cheap: pace work and the lag ladder happen with the gamer ball model only. And if that blue IS the same model as the white — then the scatter has no ball excuse, and the foot-powder strike test just became more interesting.

THE HONEST CAVEATS. An above-ground base STOPS a ball that touches it — some of the nine dead finishes would have trickled a foot past on a real green, so 'dead at base' means make-or-tap-in, not perfect dying weight; the tracked arrivals all came in soft with no ricochet, so none were hot. Balls can carry over between clips, and every parked ball was counted once — the set-E correction above is exactly that rule doing its job. And direction is still unscored: left/right of the base in any frame here is camera geometry, not a miss pattern.

THE EVENING MAT SESSION — DIRECTION, AT LAST. Five clips arrived from an indoor lined mat (19:54), three putts on the LINK.2.1 shot from two angles, both ALONG the target line: down-the-line from floor level behind the ball (img0015/16/17, one clip per putt) and reverse down-the-line from the hole end (IMG_3476, img3478). A sixth clip is still to come.

These are the RIGHT angles, and that is worth saying after a session of 23 oblique clips settled nothing. A camera on the target line is what makes start line measurable, and the mat supplies a printed centre line to measure against. Two putts were tracked frame by frame, with the ball's own 1.68" diameter setting the scale at every depth. The reference checks out: a stationary printed dash ON the centre line reads 0.00" offset in both clips, so the method is unbiased to about a thirtieth of an inch.

THE THIRD CLIP LANDED, so all three putts are measured from the hole end (IMG_3476, img3477, img3478 — one putt each) with the down-the-line set (img0015/16/17) as the matching pair. PUTT A (IMG_3476) rolled DEAD STRAIGHT — within about 0.1" of the printed line for its entire visible roll, which is roughly 0.8° and inside the measurement noise. PUTT B (img3478) started on the line and drifted steadily to the LEFT, reaching about 1.0–1.3" left by the time it got to the hole — call it 1°. So: one square, one a degree left, no consistent bias across the two.

Set that against the Jul 30 baseline of 1.5–1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts and it is a genuine improvement. It is also two putts, with an uncertainty of roughly ±0.5° once lens distortion and motion blur are allowed for, so it is encouraging rather than conclusive.

ALL THREE, AND THE SHAPE OF IT CHANGED. Putt A ran about 0.8° RIGHT of the printed line (0.09" at the hole). Putt B ran about 1.0° LEFT (1.33"). Putt C started dead on the line and finished about 0.6° RIGHT (0.17"). Mean bias: roughly 0.1° right, which is zero. Median miss: 0.8°.

That is a different fault from the one on the card. Jul 30 measured 1.5° LEFT, 1.7° LEFT and one straight — three putts pulling the same way, which is what an AIM error looks like, because aim does not change between reps. Tonight is 0.8 right, 1.0 left, 0.6 right — scattered either side of zero. The one-way pull did not reproduce on any of the three.

So the signature left miss, measured, is GONE from these putts, and what is sitting in its place is DISPERSION. That distinction is worth more than the improvement itself, because the two point at different causes. A bias points at aim, and the barely-open setup is the obvious candidate for having removed it. A two-way scatter points at something that varies stroke to stroke — and the leading candidate, unmeasured on all four putters Jack has owned this month, is STRIKE LOCATION. Heel and toe contact rotate the face in opposite directions, which is exactly a scatter with no bias. That is an inference, not a measurement, and the foot-powder test settles it in twelve minutes.

By the project's own gate — median inside 0.5° — this does NOT come off the card. 0.8° is better than 1.6° and it is not yet passed.
detail.compare:
Beekman (Aug 1) said pace felt dialled; it was a feeling, from a scramble, on slow greens, with no camera. This is ~20 measured finishes landing on the same side: the pace curve is real, and the LINK matched the DF3i from every distance it was given. What today adds that Beekman couldn't: the short range — the closing 6–8 ft set went dead three times out of five with a 5-incher besides, and the five-foot DF3i set clustered inside 2.5 ft.

Against the Jul 30 indoor sessions, the same trade as before: the mat measured DIRECTION but had no green; today measured DISTANCE but has no line. The two halves of the diagnosis still haven't been in the same shot.

On the head-to-head, the sets never played the same putt from the same spot, so nothing ranks the putters — but both heads posting dead finishes everywhere means neither head is the variable that mattered today. The stroke behind them did the work. The one variable that DID separate results was the ball.

AND THE HALVES MET — partly. The line above about the two halves of the diagnosis never being in the same shot is now half-answered: Jul 30 measured direction indoors, the Aug 10 afternoon measured distance outdoors, and the Aug 10 evening measured direction again, on the first putts filmed since the barely-open discovery. What is still true is that direction has only ever been measured INDOORS, on a mat with a printed line, and distance has only ever been measured OUTDOORS. Neither session has yet measured both at once, and the mat is the reason the direction half keeps looking better than the scorecard does.
detail.limits:
THE CAVEAT THAT DECIDES WHAT THIS IS WORTH: this was a mat with a printed target line, and a printed line does the AIMING for you. The oldest unexplained split in this whole project is 10/10 start lines on the mat against a left miss that only ever shows up on the course, and the barely-open discovery is an explanation for exactly that split — an AIM error, not a stroke error. So this session tests whether the stroke can send the ball down a line it has been handed. It cannot test whether Jack aims correctly when nothing is drawn on the ground, which is the open question. Three putts on a lined mat are consistent with the aim hypothesis and do not confirm it. Note the scatter makes this sharper rather than softer: if the remaining misses are strike-driven, they will show up on a green too, because a printed line cannot fix where the ball meets the face.

FACE ANGLE IS NOT MEASURABLE IN THIS FOOTAGE. The putter head spans about 70 pixels in the reverse clip; a 1.5° rotation of the face would move its ends by under two pixels, well below the noise. Jack's read that these are small numbers is correct and, if anything, understated.

entries.text: PUTTING — CONFIRM THE PULL STAYS GONE, then stop working on this. Scope cut Aug 10 after the three mat putts came back with no directional bias (0.8° right, 1.0° left, 0.6° right against Jul 30's 1.5–1.7° LEFT). The barely-open setup did what it was supposed to do. ONE CHECK LEFT: five putts at a real target — a coin or a tee on a practice green, nothing drawn on the ground — filmed from directly behind the ball on the line. You are looking for ONE thing: do the misses still fall on both sides? If yes, this closes and start line stops being tracked. Do NOT chase magnitude — a 0.8° miss still holes out to nearly eight feet, the old 0.5° target was too strict for a phone measurement carrying ±0.5° of its own error, and it has been retired. KEEP THE FEEL AS IT IS: don't retrain the aim picture with a mirror on top of it, or you apply the correction twice and the miss reappears on the right. Worth re-checking the feel monthly so it doesn't drift, but it is no longer a priority item — pace is.

briefing.focus: You feel better with the weight BACK while the ball sits forward — and you've heard the weight is supposed to be forward. Here's what that combination costs, why it lands on the fault still open on your card, and how to settle it with evidence instead of dogma. REWRITTEN Aug 10: the DF3i has been RETURNED, so every instruction here that was tuned to its Press Pistol 2° grip is out — including 'hands ahead at impact', which is now wrong on the putter in your bag. This version also finally states the ball position, which the plans had quietly stopped doing.

sections.t: What 'weight forward' is actually for
sections.b: It isn't a rule for its own sake. Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the putter meets the ball. That's the whole mechanism — everything below follows from it, on any head.
sections.k: Lead-side pressure does one job: it pins where the stroke bottoms out.

sections.t: The cost — loft, hop, skid, short
sections.b:
Ball forward is correct. But weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so by the time the putter arrives the head is climbing hard and the shaft is leaning AWAY from the target. That adds loft you never asked for. The ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then starts rolling. Every bit of that hop is energy that was supposed to become roll — so the putt arrives soft. Worse, the skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your PACE stops being repeatable from green to green.

Note how narrow the window is on THIS head. The LINK carries 2° of effective loft. That is all you have. Lean away from the target and you add to it; lean toward the target and you take it below zero and drive the ball down. Both ends of that mistake produce the same symptom — a ball that skids before it rolls and finishes short of what the stroke intended.
sections.k: Hanging back adds loft, and added loft makes the ball hop, skid and arrive short.

sections.t: Why this is your fault, specifically
sections.b:
Read the card as it stands Aug 10. Path: settled. Tempo: settled at 2.0:1. Start line: the one-way left pull did NOT reproduce across three measured putts — that fault has been downgraded. The one thing wide open is PACE, and it is not a small thing: it benched a putter on Jul 30, reprieved it on Aug 1 and RETURNED it on Aug 10, three verdicts in eleven days without a single calibrated lag session behind any of them.

Hop-and-skid off a low point in the wrong place is the textbook cause of exactly that signature — lags that arrive soft and a distance that won't repeat between surfaces. Your stroke is no longer the problem. Where the arc bottoms out, and where on the face you catch it, still might be.
sections.k: Pace is your one open fault, which is exactly what a wandering low point damages.

sections.t: The second cost — the pull
sections.b: Sitting back drops the trail shoulder and slides your EYELINE behind the ball. Eyes behind the ball make you see the line right of where it truly is, and you square it up with a whisker of pull. Both real misses in the Stage-0 block settled on the PULL side — logged there as a lean, not proof. This belongs on that candidate-cause list.
sections.k: Weight back also leaves the face open through impact — a second route to a missed line.

sections.t: The third cost — the flip can come back
sections.b:
Hanging back leaves the hands drifting behind where they started through impact. Hands falling back = the wrists want to save it = a flick, and that flick was the engine of the old blow-through left miss. Zero-torque has buried that miss on film across three heads now, and the Aug 10 measurements say the left pull is gone — but this is the one setup that can wake it up.

One thing genuinely improved when the DF3i went back. Its Press Pistol 2° was leaning the shaft forward while your hands hung back behind it, and something had to give — the grip and the setup were fighting each other. The Pistol 0 has no built-in lean at all, so there is nothing pulling against you. The address the putter wants and the address you naturally take are now the same address.
sections.k: Hands behind the ball invite a wrist flick, the old engine of the blow-through miss.

sections.t: Before changing anything — feel isn't real
sections.b: Your own Golf Mind note states the principle: 'Hands over the ball: it FEELS like a forward press, but it isn't.' The same illusion runs in reverse. Weight that FEELS back is often pressure that's actually close to neutral — and neutral may be perfectly fine. Don't discard a setup you putt well from on the strength of a feel. FILM IT FACE-ON first. That single clip also closes the early-lift fault, the last open item from Session 8.
sections.k: Feel isn't evidence. Film it before you change anything, because comfort lies.

sections.t: What has to be true (the real checklist)
sections.b:
Forget 'weight forward' as a slogan. Four things actually matter, and you can keep your comfort as long as they hold.

(1) BALL ONE TO TWO BALL-WIDTHS INSIDE THE LEAD HEEL. This is the number the plans had stopped giving you.

(2) LOW POINT at or just behind the ball, so the head is a HAIR ascending at contact — that slight upstroke is what produces true roll. This is the one that ball position is FOR.

(3) SHAFT RETURNS TO VERTICAL at impact — the same place it started. REWRITTEN Aug 10: this rule used to read 'hands level with or a touch ahead of the ball, never behind it', which was correct for the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° and is wrong for the putter you now own. See the section below.

(4) PRESSURE around 55/45 lead — enough to anchor the low point, not so much that you start steering. If your weight-back feel still delivers 1 through 3, keep it.
sections.k: Four things: ball 1–2 balls inside the lead heel, low point just behind it, shaft back to vertical at impact, 55/45.

sections.t: Ball position, and the hands rule that inverted
sections.k: 1–2 ball-widths inside the lead heel — and 'hands 1.35" behind' is zero lean, not a position you set.
sections.b:
BALL POSITION — the number, since the plans had stopped saying it: ONE TO TWO BALL-WIDTHS INSIDE YOUR LEAD HEEL. Forward of centre, so the head is a hair ASCENDING when it reaches the ball. Trust the ground reference over the body one: 'off the left breast' points at the same spot and has been the wording for weeks, but a breast/armpit line moves when your posture changes, and your deep-bend, stand-close setup is exactly the kind of posture that moves it. The heel doesn't move. On the mat, mark it.

AND THE THING THAT READS LIKE A CONTRADICTION, because two plans said opposite-sounding things. 'Hands ~1.35" behind the ball' and 'hands never behind the ball' are not in conflict — they are different variables at different moments.

The 1.35" is NOT a stance instruction and it is not something you set. It is what a VERTICAL SHAFT produces on this putter, and the arithmetic is exact: the ball's centre sits half a ball (0.84") beyond the face, and on a heel-shafted blade with a riser hosel the face sits roughly half an inch forward of the shaft axis. Add them and the hands land about 1.35" behind the ball centre. That IS zero lean. It happens by itself if you don't manipulate it.

'Hands ahead at impact' was a PRESS PISTOL 2° rule and it went back with the DF3i. That grip built 2° of lean in, so the hands finished slightly ahead by design. The LINK's 2° of effective loft is built to be delivered at 0° LEAN — so on this putter, hands ahead at impact DELOFTS it, drives the ball into the turf, and buys you the hop-and-skid this plan exists to prevent. What you want is the shaft RETURNING TO VERTICAL at impact: the same place it started, not ahead of it.

The half of the old rule that survives is the other direction — the hands must not fall FURTHER back, and the wrists must not flick. Zero lean is the target. Negative lean is still the old enemy.

sections.t: The forgiveness is gone — stakes back up
sections.b:
This section has now flipped twice, so here is where it actually stands. The DF3i — wide, deep, high-MOI, genuinely forgiving of a low point that wandered — was RETURNED on Aug 10. What's in your hands is the LINK.2.1: a narrow blade with far less MOI, where a strike off the middle bleeds more ball speed and every instruction above carries more weight.

So the stakes go back UP, and none of the instructions change. Low point pinned at or just behind the ball, shaft returning to vertical: on a mallet those were worth a little consistency; on this blade they are the difference between a lag that finishes and one that dies four feet short.

The compensation is that a blade REPORTS a bad strike where a mallet MUFFLES it. That is genuinely useful right now — your feel is a better instrument on this head than it was on the last one. It is also why the tape test moved up the queue: if the low point or the strike is wandering, this putter will tell you, and foot powder will show you where.
sections.k: The mallet that covered for a wandering low point has been returned. The blade reports what it muffled.

sections.t: Settle it with data
sections.b:
A/B LAG LADDER — 30 feet, two blocks of 10. Block A: your current feel. Block B: the change you're testing, everything else identical. Mark where each ball STOPS and measure the spread. Tighter spread wins — that's the answer, not anyone's opinion. SOUND TEST: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a hopping ball adds a faint scuff a beat later — listen for the scuff. FACE-ON CLIP: what it now has to show is the shaft RETURNING TO VERTICAL rather than arriving ahead, where the head bottoms out relative to the ball, and ball position rep to rep. Note the change from the old version of this line: on the Press Pistol 2° you expected to see lean already at address and the question was whether it held. On the Pistol 0 there is no lean at address, so whatever the tape shows IS the press.

Ball position is settled above and no longer an open question — one to two ball-widths inside the lead heel, marked on the mat. The ladder is the measuring protocol for any future change. And it is the FIRST thing that gets run, not a follow-up: this putter's power curve has never been built, pace is the fault that just cost you a head, and you may as well build the curve with the low point in the right place.
sections.k: A/B it on the mat and let the stopping points decide, not the feel.

rules: Ball ONE TO TWO BALL-WIDTHS inside the lead heel — that's the number
Lead-side pressure has ONE job: pinning the low point
Low point at or just behind the ball = a hair ascending = true roll
Shaft RETURNS TO VERTICAL at impact — not ahead of the ball
Hands ~1.35" behind is what zero lean LOOKS like, not a position to set
The blade REPORTS a bad strike — the mallet that muffled it is gone

briefing.focus: UPDATED Aug 10, and this is the last grip flip — the DF3i and its Press Pistol 2° have been RETURNED, so 'hands even with the ball' is retired for good. The LINK.2.1's Pistol 0 has no built-in lean: shaft VERTICAL, hands ~1.35" BEHIND the ball. New this update and the biggest thing on the card in weeks — you've found that setting the face BARELY OPEN at address is the sweet spot. That is very likely not a compensation but a correction, and it points straight at the fault this project opened with. Everything that came off film of YOUR stroke is unchanged: GET LOW, TRAIL FOOT back, rock the shoulders.

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.b: Your words, and they go at the top of the plan rather than the bottom of a setup list: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you only carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one — not the press, not the rehearsals, not the pace word. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.
sections.k: Bend over and get low — that's the anchor feel everything else hangs off.

sections.t: Why the bend is more than comfort
sections.b:
Two real mechanisms sit under that feel. FIRST — the LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at the lie angle it was built for. Stand too tall or too far away and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its designed lie, and the zero-torque property this whole project was built on quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology. On this head the built spec is 69° lie, 2° effective loft and 0° shaft lean, with an aluminium riser hosel sized to the lie angle — still confirm the length is 34". SECOND — more bend lets the arms hang freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall flattens that plane and builds an arc into the stroke you don't want.

This one carried across every head change, because it's a property of you and your posture rather than of whatever is in your hands.
sections.k: The bend isn't comfort: it presents the lie the putter needs, and steepens the shoulder plane that makes the stroke straight.

sections.t: The setup
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. Ball ONE TO TWO BALL-WIDTHS INSIDE THE LEAD HEEL (this is the same spot the old 'off the left breast' cue was pointing at — the heel is just a reference that doesn't move when your posture does). Weight stacked ON the ball — pressure over it, not on the trail foot. TRAIL FOOT a touch BACK — it creeps forward on its own and opens you. Rock the shoulders, no hands. Loose grip. Face set BARELY OPEN — see the section below.

THE HANDS CUE, FINAL VERSION. HANDS ~1.35" BEHIND THE BALL, shaft DEAD VERTICAL. The DF3i went back on Aug 10 and its Press Pistol 2° went with it, so the 'hands even with the ball, the grip supplies the lean' rule is retired — there is no longer a grip in your bag that it describes.

The LINK's Pistol 0 has zero built-in press, and this is measured rather than assumed: overhead stills on Jul 30 put the shaft essentially vertical and repeatable to 0.3° across 59 frames, with the hands about 1.35" behind the ball. That is the geometry L.A.B. built this putter around — 69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° lean — not a flaw in your address to be corrected. Don't manufacture lean with your hands to make it look like a normal putter. With only 2° of effective loft there is almost nothing to deloft before you're driving the ball into the turf, and a driven ball skids before it rolls, which costs you most on exactly the long putts you're trying to control.

ONE ADDITION, because pace is the live priority: mark that ball position and keep it there, same spot every rep. Forward of centre puts the head a hair ASCENDING at contact, which is what produces true roll; launch is sensitive to where the ball sits relative to the low point, and a position that wanders reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine.

AND DON'T READ THE 1.35" AS A BALL-POSITION INSTRUCTION — it isn't one. It's what a vertical shaft produces: the ball's centre sits half a ball (0.84") beyond the face, and the face sits about half an inch forward of the shaft axis on a riser-hosel blade. That sums to ~1.35", and it happens by itself if you don't manipulate it. Ball position is set by your FEET; shaft lean is set by your HANDS. Full detail, including why the old 'hands ahead at impact' rule inverted when the DF3i went back, is in Putting Setup — Weight & Low Point.
sections.k: Hands ~1.35" BEHIND the ball and the shaft vertical — the Pistol 0 has no lean to borrow, and none to add.

sections.t: THE PRESS — settled from first principles
sections.b:
Start from what you are actually holding. The Pistol 0 is an UNPRESSED grip — zero built-in forward lean, shaft vertical, hands behind the ball. So unlike the DF3i era, the soft press is now the ONLY source of shaft lean in your stroke.

That changes the arithmetic in your favour and it's worth being precise about why, because the old rule was reasoned from real numbers. On the Press Pistol 2° there was already lean built in, so any press you added STACKED on top of it and could push effective loft below zero — a putter delivering negative loft drives the ball down into the green instead of rolling it. That is why 'keep it tiny' was a hard rule for the whole DF3i era.

With the Pistol 0 there is nothing to stack on. A small press cannot drive loft below zero, because it is starting from zero lean and 2° of loft. So the hard 'tiny or else' rule is genuinely suspended.

What replaces it is a softer rule with a different reason, and the reason is pace — see below. Do not read 'suspended' as 'manufacture some lean'. The putter is designed around 0° and there is very little loft to give away.
sections.k: The Pistol 0 has no lean to stack on, so the hard 'tiny or else' rule is suspended — but consistency replaces it, for pace.

sections.t: What this putter needs from the setup
sections.b:
A lie-angle-balanced putter makes one demand of you and it is not a stroke demand: present the shaft at the lie it was built for. Get that wrong — stand tall, reach for it — and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its designed lie, and the self-squaring property you bought degrades. That is why the deep bend matters mechanically here and not just for comfort.

Everything else in this routine came from film of YOUR stroke — path, shoulder plane, stance line, trigger — so none of it is putter-specific and none of it changed when the mallet went back. Two things ARE this head's business. The lie presentation above. And your AIM PICTURE: a narrow blade topline frames the target very differently from the wide mallet you spent nine days looking at, which is one reason the barely-open find is worth nailing down with a number now rather than trusting the eye through another head change.

One more that is specific to this head: the riser hosel. The shaft is NOT a reliable pointer to where the head's mass sits, so don't use it to judge the sweet spot by eye — that's what the tap test is for.
sections.k: Present the shaft at its built lie and re-check your aim picture. Leave the stroke alone.

sections.t: THE FACE — barely open is your square
sections.k: On a zero-torque head the face points where you set it, so this reads as an aim correction, not a compensation — which would make it the answer to the oldest fault on the card.
sections.b:
Your find, Aug 10: setting the face BARELY OPEN at address is the sweet spot. Take it seriously, because there is a clean mechanism underneath it and it lines up with everything already measured.

Start from what a zero-torque putter can and cannot do. Lie Angle Balance means the face does not TWIST during the stroke — and Jul 30 film confirmed exactly that, the face held. What it cannot do is decide where the face POINTS. A zero-torque head faithfully delivers whatever angle you set at address. So on this putter, face-at-impact is very close to face-at-address, by design.

Now put the two facts together. Overhead film measured the face pointing 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT at impact on two of three putts — the only hard number behind your signature miss. On a head that doesn't twist, a face pointing left at impact was almost certainly pointing left AT ADDRESS. That reframes the whole fault: it is an AIM error, not a delivery error. Nothing is closing through impact — you were aiming there the whole time.

And that is precisely what 'barely open feels right' means. What reads as barely open to your eyes is, on the actual target line, square. You are not compensating for a moving face; you are correcting a perception. That matters enormously for whether this holds up: compensations for timing drift and have to be re-found every week, but an aim offset is stable. This one should keep working.

It also answers the aim-check item directly. Your stance measured SQUARE on overhead film — the toe line ran 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED across three reps, never open — so the leak was never in your feet. The instruction was to look higher. The face itself is higher, and here it is.

sections.t: The trap — don't stack the two fixes
sections.k: 'Barely open' is a feel calibrated to your current aim picture; retrain the picture as well and you'll start missing right.
sections.b:
This is the one way the discovery goes wrong, and it's worth reading before the next practice green.

'Barely open' is not a measurement. It is a FEEL, and it works because it is calibrated against your current, slightly-left aim perception. Which means there are two different fixes available for the same fault, and they do not combine:

LANE A — keep the feel. Aim what feels barely open, verify ONCE that it actually produces a square start line, then stop thinking about it. Cheap, fast, and it's already working.

LANE B — retrain the aim picture with a mirror or a laser until genuinely square LOOKS square, and drop the 'barely open' language entirely.

Do BOTH and you have applied the correction twice: a face that is genuinely open, and a new miss to the RIGHT. Pick a lane. Lane A is the recommendation — you found it yourself, on the course, and the cheapest fix is the one that's already in your hands.

The second hazard is drift, and this project has a documented history with it. A feel with no number attached wanders, and it wanders toward the exaggeration — 'barely open' quietly becomes 'open' over a few weeks, and the miss reappears on the other side without an obvious cause. So put a number on it once, then re-check it monthly. That's the new action item, and it's five putts long.

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — the alignment leak
sections.b: Self-reported Jul 29 and worth taking seriously: your right foot creeps UP — forward, toward the target line — and it drags the stance line open with it. Open the feet and the shoulders follow, so you end up aimed LEFT of where you think you are. The fix is exactly what you said: set that trail foot a touch further back than feels natural. Expect it to feel CLOSED, like you're aimed right. That feeling is the correction, not an error — you're recalibrating off an open baseline, so square will read as closed until it beds in. Trust the line you set, not the feel, for the first few sessions.
sections.k: Your trail foot creeps forward, opens the stance and aims you left. Set it back — square will feel closed.

sections.t: Why it wrecks the takeaway specifically
sections.b: Because in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. There's no arc to absorb a misaligned setup — 'straight back' is straight back along whatever line your shoulders are on, so an open stance doesn't just aim you left, it points the whole stroke left. Then one of two things happens, and both are bad: you feel it immediately and manipulate the takeaway to save it, which puts the HANDS back in charge of a stroke built to have no hands in it — or you don't, and the ball starts left. That's why a stance error shows up as a takeaway problem. The takeaway is fine; it's obeying a line that's wrong.
sections.k: In a straight stroke the shoulder line IS the track, so an open stance points the whole stroke left.

sections.t: This is the miss the putter can't fix
sections.b:
Your signature miss is LEFT on short putts — the through-line of the entire putter saga, and it has now outlived four putters. That history is what rules the HEAD out: a fault that survives four different putters was never about the putter.

What it never ruled out was aim. A perfectly square face aimed at a target left of the hole produces exactly this miss, and no putter ever built will save you from it. Zero-torque guarantees the FACE stays square; it cannot guarantee the face is square TO THE RIGHT THING. That has been the standing line in this plan for two weeks, and the barely-open find is the first thing to actually act on it.

Note the split that always made the case: your 10-ball blocks started 10/10 on line on the MAT, where an alignment aid is doing the aiming for you, while the miss kept showing up on the COURSE, where nothing is. That pattern is an aim signature, not a stroke signature. It has been sitting in the data the whole time.
sections.k: A square face aimed at the wrong target still misses left — and the mat-versus-course split says that's exactly what's been happening.

sections.t: The check that costs nothing
sections.b: Lay a club or an alignment stick down the target line just outside the ball on the practice green and set up to it — your toes should run PARALLEL to it, not converging toward it. Ten seconds, and it recalibrates the feel. The structural safeguard is already in your routine: aim the FACE to the spot FIRST, then build the stance around it. Keep that order religiously. If you build the stance first, the face gets aimed to a crooked body; if you aim the face first and the stance then creeps, the mismatch shows up as discomfort — and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.
sections.k: Alignment stick on the practice green: toes parallel, not converging. Ten seconds, recalibrates the feel.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — settled: soft press, moved with the body
sections.b:
Keep the soft press — a genuinely small one, made as the body starts to move. Its JOB is rhythm: it breaks inertia so the stroke starts as a motion rather than a decision.

On the Pistol 0 it is also the only lean in the stroke, since the grip supplies none. That makes it more honest than it was during the DF3i era — what you feel is what the shaft is doing, with nothing built in underneath it — and it makes repeatability the whole game. Nothing is masking a press that grows.

It should pass THROUGH, not be held. Held presses were a real problem on Jul 29 and the mechanism that made them dangerous is gone, but the habit isn't, and on this grip a held press drags your hands forward out of the hands-behind address the putter is built around.
sections.k: Keep the soft press for rhythm — on this grip it's the only lean in the stroke, so make it the same size every time.

sections.t: The one rule — softness IS the safeguard
sections.b:
REWRITTEN Aug 10. The old version of this rule was arithmetic: the Press Pistol's 2° meant a firm press pushed effective loft below zero. That grip has gone back with the DF3i, so that specific danger is gone.

The rule survives anyway, for a better reason. SAME PRESS, SAME SIZE, EVERY PUTT. A press that varies is a shaft lean that varies, which is a launch that varies, which is a PACE that varies — and pace is now the priority fault on the card, the one that just cost you a putter. Consistency is no longer about protecting loft from going negative; it's about not injecting a random variable into the exact thing you're trying to measure on the ladder.

Two drift signals to watch, unchanged: if the press starts to feel FIRM, or like a POSITION you sit in rather than a motion you pass through, it has crept back toward a hold. A held press also quietly moves your hands forward of the 1.35"-behind address this putter wants.
sections.k: Same press, same size, every putt — a varying press is a varying pace, and pace is the fault that just cost you a putter.

sections.t: If it creeps back into a hold
sections.b: The alternatives stay on the shelf rather than getting deleted, because you may want one later: THE FLOAT — lift the head a hair off the turf before takeaway; no hand action at all and it removes ground friction. THE WHOLE-PUTTER WAGGLE — small forward-and-back from the shoulders, wrists silent. THE LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE — a soft downward press of the shoulder that already runs the stroke. THE TRAIL-KNEE KICK — furthest from the hands, and the same trigger your full-swing routine uses. Any of them will break inertia without the hands touching shaft lean. You don't need one right now.
sections.k: Alternatives on the shelf if the press ever creeps back into a hold — float, waggle, shoulder settle, knee kick.

sections.t: How to tell it's releasing
sections.b: One face-on clip settles it: compare shaft lean at ADDRESS with shaft lean at IMPACT. Close to equal means the soft press is passing through the way it should. Meaningfully more at impact means it's being carried in, whatever it felt like — and feel is exactly what got this wrong the first time. The free check needs no camera: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click, a ball driven down into the green adds a faint scuff a beat later. Listen for the scuff.
sections.k: One face-on clip settles it: shaft lean at address versus at impact. No camera? Listen for the scuff.

sections.t: Stop shopping
sections.b:
Straight talk, because you called it yourself. Four putters in a month: the Phantom 7.5 returned Jul 20, the DF3i in Jul 18, out Jul 30, back in Aug 1, returned Aug 10, and the LINK.2.1 in and out and in again around it.

The LINK is now the only zero-torque head you own, and it is still inside its own return window. So 'stop shopping' is not quite available as advice — there is a real decision still to make. What IS available is the standard for making it: the DF3i was benched on a feeling, reprieved on a feeling, and returned on a feeling, without a single calibrated lag session behind any of the three. That is the pattern to break, not the putter.

So the rule from here, unchanged in spirit and sharper in practice: the next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag. And if this head does go back, let a scoreboard send it — two weeks of ladder data and a tape sheet — rather than a feeling. That would be the first equipment decision in this whole project with evidence under it.
sections.k: Four putters in a month, all judged on feel — break the pattern, not the putter: the next thing that changes should be a number.

sections.t: Why beside the ball and not behind it
sections.b: Rehearsing in your true putting posture — same deep bend, same arm hang, same shoulder plane — means the stroke that FEELS like 30 feet is the stroke you actually make. Magnitude transfers one-to-one. Rehearsing from behind the ball reads the break better, but you're standing upright there, so the size you feel is only an approximation. Your open fault is pace magnitude, not reading: path ✓, face ✓, start lines 10/10 twice over. Optimise the thing that's broken.
sections.k: Rehearse in your real posture beside the ball, because magnitude transfers one-to-one that way.

sections.t: Keep the order of the two rehearsals
sections.b: Ball-look first (path and contact), hole-look second (pace). The last thing you feel is the thing you carry in — so the pace stroke must be the last one. If the hole stroke ever drifts to first, the pace feel gets overwritten by the contact feel and you're back to guessing distance. Finish rehearsal 2 WITH the soft press, at its real size: it's the one part of the stroke that never used to get a practice rep, which is how it drifted last time without you noticing.
sections.k: Ball-look first, hole-look second — the last thing you feel is what you carry in.

sections.t: Two rules underneath it
sections.b: SAME BEAT COUNT, EVERY PUTT — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts where you take an extra look are the ones that come up short. And a VERBAL BACKSTOP is worth testing: say the pace intention right before the press ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays, a word doesn't.
sections.k: Same beat count every putt, and try saying the pace intention out loud before the press.

sections.t: Still to test — lags
sections.b:
This is the top of the card, and it is the single thing that would have prevented the entire detour. The Jul 29 round was lags coming up SHORT and short putts running HOT, which is not two faults but one: a power curve you hadn't learned, so you under-hit the long ones and over-hit the short ones. That got the DF3i benched. It was never once tested. And on Aug 10 the same untested complaint sent that putter back for good.

So the curve gets built on the LINK, deliberately. The block test, twice a week: 10 balls from 30 feet. Log THREE numbers — how many finish SHORT (target no more than 1 in 10), the SPREAD front-to-back of the ten stopping points (target inside 6 feet), and the GREEN SPEED. Then the calibration set: 20, 30 and 40 feet, three balls each, noting where the BACKSTROKE ends for each distance. Written down, that mapping is the curve you have never had.

Two things make this more promising than it sounds. Tempo is already right on this head — 2.0:1 measured against a 2:1 target — so the missing ingredient is stroke LENGTH, not rhythm. And strike location has never been measured on any putter you own, which matters here because an off-centre hit bleeds ball speed and shows up as exactly this fault. The tape test is twelve minutes and it belongs at the front of this queue.

ONE WATCH ITEM from the barely-open find: if you were unconsciously steering the stroke to save a face aimed left, then fixing the aim removes the need for the steer — and a stroke that no longer steers can deliver different pace. So take a ladder reading EARLY, before the new aim beds in, and don't confuse a pace change caused by the aim fix with one caused by the putter.
sections.k: Build the power curve on the LINK — and take a reading early, because fixing the aim may move your pace too.

steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. Finish it with the soft press.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot first and set it BARELY OPEN, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → soft press with the body → putt
rules: GET LOW — the deep bend is what presents the lie this putter needs
Ball 1–2 BALL-WIDTHS inside the lead heel
Set the face BARELY OPEN — that's your square, and it's the first thing to move the left miss
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
Hands ~1.35" BEHIND the ball — the Pistol 0 has no lean, so don't add any
Press SMALL and the SAME SIZE every putt — a varying press is a varying pace

briefing.focus: UPDATED Aug 10 pm, and three things changed at once. THE SOFT PRESS IS GONE — you've taken it out entirely. HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER, straight shaft, QUIET HANDS. And you're trialling a CLAW on short putts. The first two are the same instruction from two directions and they match the film exactly, which is the good news below. Everything that came off film of YOUR stroke is unchanged: GET LOW, TRAIL FOOT back, rock the shoulders, face BARELY OPEN.

sections.t: Feel versus real — how this plan is written
sections.k: Your words set the intent; the film sets the positions. Where they disagree, the film wins.
sections.b:
Standing rule from Aug 10, in your words: the film study is king. What you say is feel, feel isn't always right, and what the film shows is the best evidence available.

The split this file uses. What YOU are doing — taking the press out, trialling a claw, aiming barely open — is yours and it's authoritative; nobody else can report your intent. Where a POSITION or a SENSATION is claimed — how open the face is, where your hands sit, whether pace felt dialled — the measurement outranks the description, and where there's no measurement the plan says so instead of guessing.

Tonight is the clean example, and it went the good way. 'Hands over the ball' and 'hands over the HEAD of the putter' are different positions — the first is forward lean, the second is a vertical shaft — and the correction landed exactly on what the Jul 30 stills measured. The feel was right; the first wording wasn't. That's the whole reason for the rule.

It cuts the other way too. 'Barely open' is still a feel with no number on it, and 'pace felt dialled' on Aug 1 is what un-benched a putter that went back nine days later. Where the film is silent, so is this plan.

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.b: Your words, and they go at the top of the plan rather than the bottom of a setup list: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you only carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one — not the press, not the rehearsals, not the pace word. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.
sections.k: Bend over and get low — that's the anchor feel everything else hangs off.

sections.t: Why the bend is more than comfort
sections.b:
Two real mechanisms sit under that feel. FIRST — the LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at the lie angle it was built for. Stand too tall or too far away and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its designed lie, and the zero-torque property this whole project was built on quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology. On this head the built spec is 69° lie, 2° effective loft and 0° shaft lean, with an aluminium riser hosel sized to the lie angle — still confirm the length is 34". SECOND — more bend lets the arms hang freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall flattens that plane and builds an arc into the stroke you don't want.

This one carried across every head change, because it's a property of you and your posture rather than of whatever is in your hands.
sections.k: The bend isn't comfort: it presents the lie the putter needs, and steepens the shoulder plane that makes the stroke straight.

sections.t: The setup
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. Ball ONE TO TWO BALL-WIDTHS INSIDE THE LEAD HEEL (this is the same spot the old 'off the left breast' cue was pointing at — the heel is just a reference that doesn't move when your posture does). Weight stacked ON the ball — pressure over it, not on the trail foot. TRAIL FOOT a touch BACK — it creeps forward on its own and opens you. Rock the shoulders, no hands. Loose grip. Face set BARELY OPEN — see the section below.

THE HANDS CUE, IN YOUR WORDS NOW: HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER. Shaft straight up and down. The DF3i went back on Aug 10 and its Press Pistol 2° went with it, so the 'hands even with the ball, the grip supplies the lean' rule is retired — there is no longer a grip in your bag that it describes.

The LINK's Pistol 0 has zero built-in press, and this is measured rather than assumed: overhead stills on Jul 30 put the shaft essentially vertical and repeatable to 0.3° across 59 frames, with the hands about 1.35" behind the ball. That is the geometry L.A.B. built this putter around — 69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° lean — not a flaw in your address to be corrected. Don't manufacture lean with your hands to make it look like a normal putter. With only 2° of effective loft there is almost nothing to deloft before you're driving the ball into the turf, and a driven ball skids before it rolls, which costs you most on exactly the long putts you're trying to control.

ONE ADDITION, because pace is the live priority: mark that ball position and keep it there, same spot every rep. Forward of centre puts the head a hair ASCENDING at contact, which is what produces true roll; launch is sensitive to where the ball sits relative to the low point, and a position that wanders reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine.

AND YOUR CUE AND THE FILM'S NUMBER ARE THE SAME THING, which is worth seeing because it is the first time a feel and a measurement in this project have landed on each other exactly. Hands over the putter HEAD means the shaft is vertical. A vertical shaft puts the hands about 1.35" behind the BALL — because the ball's centre sits half a ball (0.84") beyond the face, and the face sits about half an inch forward of the shaft axis on a riser-hosel blade. Your cue and the Jul 30 stills are describing one position from two ends. Use your version; it's easier to feel and it can't be misread.

DON'T READ THE 1.35" AS A BALL-POSITION INSTRUCTION — it isn't one. It's what a vertical shaft produces: the ball's centre sits half a ball (0.84") beyond the face, and the face sits about half an inch forward of the shaft axis on a riser-hosel blade. That sums to ~1.35", and it happens by itself if you don't manipulate it. Ball position is set by your FEET; shaft lean is set by your HANDS. Full detail, including why the old 'hands ahead at impact' rule inverted when the DF3i went back, is in Putting Setup — Weight & Low Point.
sections.k: Hands over the head of the putter — which is exactly what the film measured, from the other direction.

sections.t: THE PRESS — retired Aug 10
sections.b:
GONE, by your call, and the arithmetic backs you. This section spent three weeks arguing about how big a forward press should be. On the Pistol 0 the answer turns out to be none.

Why it lands well HERE specifically. The LINK carries 2° of effective loft and is built to deliver it at 0° shaft lean. That is the entire design. Any press adds lean, any lean subtracts loft, and there is no loft to spare — take 2° down toward zero and the putter drives the ball into the turf, it skids before it rolls, and it finishes short of what the stroke intended. On the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° there was built-in lean to reason about and a hard 'keep it tiny' rule to stop you stacking on top of it. That grip went back with the putter. With no press and no built-in lean, the shaft simply stays where it belongs.

It also removes a variable from the fault that matters most. A press that varies in size is a shaft lean that varies, which is a launch that varies, which is a PACE that varies — and pace is the open fault, the one that cost you a putter. No press means one less thing feeding it.

What you gave up is real but small, and it's covered in the trigger section below: the press had a job, and it wasn't lean.
sections.k: You've taken the press out, and on this putter that is the right call — 2° of loft has nothing to spare.

sections.t: THE CLAW — for short ones only
sections.k: It fits this putter's premise and this month's evidence — just keep it off the lags and keep the shaft vertical.
sections.b:
You're trialling a claw on short putts. Worth saying plainly: this is a better-founded idea than the last time a grip change came up, and the reasons are specific.
